# subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/subtle/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#subtle---)subtle

**Pure-Rust traits and utilities for constant-time cryptographic implementations.**

It consists of a `Choice` type, and a collection of traits using `Choice`
instead of `bool` which are intended to execute in constant-time.  The `Choice`
type is a wrapper around a `u8` that holds a `0` or `1`.

`subtle = "2.6"`This crate represents a “best-effort” attempt, since side-channels are ultimately a property of a deployed cryptographic system including the hardware it runs on, not just of software.

The traits are implemented using bitwise operations, and should execute in constant time provided that a) the bitwise operations are constant-time and b) the bitwise operations are not recognized as a conditional assignment and optimized back into a branch.

For a compiler to recognize that bitwise operations represent a conditional
assignment, it needs to know that the value used to generate the bitmasks is
really a boolean `i1` rather than an `i8` byte value. In an attempt to
prevent this refinement, the crate tries to hide the value of a `Choice`’s
inner `u8` by passing it through a volatile read. For more information, see
the *About* section below.

Rust versions from 1.51 or higher have const generics support. You may enable
`const-generics` feautre to have `subtle` traits implemented for arrays `[T; N]`.

Versions prior to `2.2` recommended use of the `nightly` feature to enable an
optimization barrier; this is not required in versions `2.2` and above.

Note: the `subtle` crate contains `debug_assert`s to check invariants during
debug builds. These invariant checks involve secret-dependent branches, and
are not present when compiled in release mode. This crate is intended to be
used in release mode.

[§](https://docs.rs#documentation)Documentation

Documentation is available [here](https://docs.rs/subtle).

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

Rust **1.41** or higher.

Minimum supported Rust version can be changed in the future, but it will be done with a minor version bump.

[§](https://docs.rs#about)About

This library aims to be the Rust equivalent of Go’s `crypto/subtle` module.

Old versions of the optimization barrier in `impl From<u8> for Choice` were
based on Tim Maclean’s [work on  rust-timing-shield](https://www.chosenplaintext.ca/open-source/rust-timing-shield/security),
which attempts to provide a more comprehensive approach for preventing
software side-channels in Rust code.
From version

`2.2`, it was based on Diane Hosfelt and Amber Sprenkels’ work on
“Secret Types in Rust”.`subtle` is authored by isis agora lovecruft and Henry de Valence.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

This code is a low-level library, intended for specific use-cases implementing cryptographic protocols. It represents a best-effort attempt to protect against some software side-channels. Because side-channel resistance is not a property of software alone, but of software together with hardware, any such effort is fundamentally limited.

**USE AT YOUR OWN RISK**

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

To get you started quickly, the easiest and highest-level way to get
a random value is to use [ random()](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html); alternatively you can use

[. The](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)

`thread_rng()`[trait provides a useful API on all RNGs, while the](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[and](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)

`distributions`[modules provide further functionality on top of RNGs.](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)

`seq````
use rand::prelude::*;
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    // Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
    println!("char: {}", rand::random::<char>());
}
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let y: f64 = rng.gen(); // generates a float between 0 and 1
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [distributions](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)
- Generating random samples from probability distributions
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Convenience re-export of common members
- [rngs](https://docs.rs/rngs/index.html)
- Random number generators and adapters
- [seq](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)
- Sequence-related functionality

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error type of random number generators

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Crypto](https://docs.rs/trait.CryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait used to indicate that an `RngCore``BlockRngCore`
- [Fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Fill.html)
- Types which may be filled with random data
- [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)
- An automatically-implemented extension trait on `RngCore`
- [RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html)
- The core of a random number generator.
- [Seedable](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html)- Rng
- A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [random](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html)- `std`and- `std_rng`
- Generates a random value using the thread-local random number generator.
- [thread_](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)- rng - `std`and- `std_rng`
- Retrieve the lazily-initialized thread-local random number generator,
seeded by the system. Intended to be used in method chaining style,
e.g. `thread_rng().gen::<i32>()`, or cached locally, e.g.`let mut rng = thread_rng();`. Invoked by the`Default`trait, making`ThreadRng::default()`equivalent.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/subtle

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#subtle---)subtle

**Pure-Rust traits and utilities for constant-time cryptographic implementations.**

It consists of a `Choice` type, and a collection of traits using `Choice`
instead of `bool` which are intended to execute in constant-time.  The `Choice`
type is a wrapper around a `u8` that holds a `0` or `1`.

`subtle = "2.6"`This crate represents a “best-effort” attempt, since side-channels are ultimately a property of a deployed cryptographic system including the hardware it runs on, not just of software.

The traits are implemented using bitwise operations, and should execute in constant time provided that a) the bitwise operations are constant-time and b) the bitwise operations are not recognized as a conditional assignment and optimized back into a branch.

For a compiler to recognize that bitwise operations represent a conditional
assignment, it needs to know that the value used to generate the bitmasks is
really a boolean `i1` rather than an `i8` byte value. In an attempt to
prevent this refinement, the crate tries to hide the value of a `Choice`’s
inner `u8` by passing it through a volatile read. For more information, see
the *About* section below.

Rust versions from 1.51 or higher have const generics support. You may enable
`const-generics` feautre to have `subtle` traits implemented for arrays `[T; N]`.

Versions prior to `2.2` recommended use of the `nightly` feature to enable an
optimization barrier; this is not required in versions `2.2` and above.

Note: the `subtle` crate contains `debug_assert`s to check invariants during
debug builds. These invariant checks involve secret-dependent branches, and
are not present when compiled in release mode. This crate is intended to be
used in release mode.

[§](https://docs.rs#documentation)Documentation

Documentation is available [here](https://docs.rs/subtle).

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

Rust **1.41** or higher.

Minimum supported Rust version can be changed in the future, but it will be done with a minor version bump.

[§](https://docs.rs#about)About

This library aims to be the Rust equivalent of Go’s `crypto/subtle` module.

Old versions of the optimization barrier in `impl From<u8> for Choice` were
based on Tim Maclean’s [work on  rust-timing-shield](https://www.chosenplaintext.ca/open-source/rust-timing-shield/security),
which attempts to provide a more comprehensive approach for preventing
software side-channels in Rust code.
From version

`2.2`, it was based on Diane Hosfelt and Amber Sprenkels’ work on
“Secret Types in Rust”.`subtle` is authored by isis agora lovecruft and Henry de Valence.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

This code is a low-level library, intended for specific use-cases implementing cryptographic protocols. It represents a best-effort attempt to protect against some software side-channels. Because side-channel resistance is not a property of software alone, but of software together with hardware, any such effort is fundamentally limited.

**USE AT YOUR OWN RISK**

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- Wrapper type which implements an optimization barrier for all accesses.
- [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html)
- The `Choice`struct represents a choice for use in conditional assignment.
- [CtOption](https://docs.rs/struct.CtOption.html)
- The `CtOption<T>`type represents an optional value similar to the`Option<T>`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- A type which can be conditionally negated in constant time.
- [Conditionally](https://docs.rs/trait.ConditionallySelectable.html)- Selectable
- A type which can be conditionally selected in constant time.
- [Constant](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html)- Time - Eq

# tokenfuse - Rust

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#tokenfuse)TokenFuse

**Runtime cost control & security for AI agents** — a drop-in proxy between
your agent and its LLM/tool providers that enforces per-run budgets, detects
runaway loops, offers a kill-switch, and keeps secrets out of the model’s
context.

This is the project’s **umbrella crate**. TokenFuse runs as a service, not a
library dependency: the gateway ships as the `tokenfuse` binary and as Docker
images on GHCR.

`docker run -p 4100:4100 -e TOKENFUSE_MODE=enforce ghcr.io/taipanbox/tokenfuse`Point your provider client at `http://127.0.0.1:4100` and attach a few
`X-Fuse-*` headers. See the [repository](https://github.com/TAIPANBOX/tokenfuse) for the full documentation, the HA
cluster, the hosted Cloud, and the MCP credential-broker.

# tatara_net - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tatara-net/0.2.127/tatara_net/

## Expand description

tatara-net: Cross-platform networking plane for the tatara cluster fabric.

The complete sandwich:

```
┌─ WASI (wasmtime) ──── Portable, sandboxed workloads ─────────┐
├─ Tatara Runtime ───── Convergence, scheduling, Raft ─────────┤
├─ eBPF (aya) ────────── Kernel hooks, pure Rust ──────────────┤
├─ WireGuard (mamorigami) ─ Encrypted mesh fabric ─────────────┤
└─ Hardware ──────────── Abstracted away ──────────────────────┘
```
On Linux: eBPF programs (XDP/TC/cgroup) for kernel-level networking. On macOS: userspace networking via tun-rs + smoltcp + hanabi proxy. Everywhere: WireGuard mesh via mamorigami for encrypted inter-node traffic.

# tatara_wasm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tatara-wasm/0.2.127/tatara_wasm/

## Expand description

`tatara-wasm` — multi-runtime WASI/WASM host for tatara guests.

Five runtimes, one trait, Cargo feature flags. Consumers pick the runtime per workload via the Lisp surface:

```
(defguest fast-fn   :kind (:wasm :runtime :wasmtime …))
(defguest k8s-fn    :kind (:wasm :runtime :wasmedge …))
(defguest embed-fn  :kind (:wasm :runtime :wamr   :features (:aot #t :no-std #t)))
```
The runtime axis is first-class — all five are shipped with
production-grade implementations in Phase H.3 (wasmtime) and
H.4 (the rest). See `docs/declarative-guests.md`.

[§](https://docs.rs#status)Status

**Phase H.1 stub.** The `WasmRuntime` enum + `WasmEngine` trait
land here now so `tatara-vm` can reference them. Runtime bodies
are empty until H.3/H.4.

# tatara_hvf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tatara-hvf/0.2.127/tatara_hvf/

## Expand description

`tatara-hvf` — Apple Hypervisor.framework backend for tatara guests.

The **bare-metal** VM engine. Direct `hv_vm_*` / `hv_vcpu_*` calls
via the `applevisor` safe-wrapper crate, own virtio device backends
(landing H.2.2), raw vCPU loop with MMIO callbacks.

[§](https://docs.rs#layering)Layering

```
  tatara-hvf (this crate)
      │  uses
      ▼
  applevisor (safe wrapper — Quarkslab)
      │  links
      ▼
  Hypervisor.framework  (aarch64-darwin only)
```
[§](https://docs.rs#cargo--build)Cargo / build

The `applevisor` dep is target-gated to `aarch64-darwin`. On any
other target, the crate compiles but `HvfEngine::new()` returns
`HvfError::UnsupportedPlatform`. This keeps `cargo check --workspace` clean on Linux CI while the real engine is only
exercised on M-series Macs.

[§](https://docs.rs#entitlements)Entitlements

Running any HVF binary requires the `com.apple.security.hypervisor`
entitlement. For `cargo test`, either codesign the test binary
with an entitlements plist or run tests as root. Currently:

```
codesign --entitlements entitlements.plist --sign - \
  target/debug/deps/tatara_hvf-*
```
A follow-up CI helper crate will encapsulate this; for now the
`vm_create_is_supported` test is `#[ignore]` by default so `cargo test` doesn’t fail when entitlements aren’t set.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use stub::`- [HvfEngine](https://docs.rs/stub/struct.HvfEngine.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [stub](https://docs.rs/stub/index.html)
- Non-aarch64-darwin stub. HVF doesn’t exist on Linux / Intel Mac, so
`HvfEngine::new()`returns a typed error. The struct still exists so downstream crates compile.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Guest](https://docs.rs/struct.GuestRegion.html)- Region
- A guest memory region mapped into the VM’s physical address space.
- [Permissions](https://docs.rs/struct.Permissions.html)
- Page permissions for a mapped region.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [HvfError](https://docs.rs/enum.HvfError.html)
- Errors from the HVF backend.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [CRATE_](https://docs.rs/constant.CRATE_STATUS.html)- STATUS

# subtle 2.6.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/subtle/2.6.1

**Pure-Rust traits and utilities for constant-time cryptographic implementations.**

It consists of a `Choice` type, and a collection of traits using `Choice`
instead of `bool` which are intended to execute in constant-time.  The `Choice`
type is a wrapper around a `u8` that holds a `0` or `1`.

```
 = "2.6"
```
This crate represents a “best-effort” attempt, since side-channels are ultimately a property of a deployed cryptographic system including the hardware it runs on, not just of software.

The traits are implemented using bitwise operations, and should execute in constant time provided that a) the bitwise operations are constant-time and b) the bitwise operations are not recognized as a conditional assignment and optimized back into a branch.

For a compiler to recognize that bitwise operations represent a conditional
assignment, it needs to know that the value used to generate the bitmasks is
really a boolean `i1` rather than an `i8` byte value. In an attempt to
prevent this refinement, the crate tries to hide the value of a `Choice`'s
inner `u8` by passing it through a volatile read. For more information, see
the *About* section below.

Rust versions from 1.51 or higher have const generics support. You may enable
`const-generics` feautre to have `subtle` traits implemented for arrays `[T; N]`.

Versions prior to `2.2` recommended use of the `nightly` feature to enable an
optimization barrier; this is not required in versions `2.2` and above.

Note: the `subtle` crate contains `debug_assert`s to check invariants during
debug builds. These invariant checks involve secret-dependent branches, and
are not present when compiled in release mode. This crate is intended to be
used in release mode.

## Documentation

Documentation is available [here](https://docs.rs/subtle).

## Minimum Supported Rust Version

Rust **1.41** or higher.

Minimum supported Rust version can be changed in the future, but it will be done with a minor version bump.

## About

This library aims to be the Rust equivalent of Go’s `crypto/subtle` module.

Old versions of the optimization barrier in `impl From<u8> for Choice` were
based on Tim Maclean's [work on  rust-timing-shield](https://www.chosenplaintext.ca/open-source/rust-timing-shield/security),
which attempts to provide a more comprehensive approach for preventing
software side-channels in Rust code.
From version

`2.2`, it was based on Diane Hosfelt and Amber Sprenkels' work on
"Secret Types in Rust".`subtle` is authored by isis agora lovecruft and Henry de Valence.

## Warning

This code is a low-level library, intended for specific use-cases implementing cryptographic protocols. It represents a best-effort attempt to protect against some software side-channels. Because side-channel resistance is not a property of software alone, but of software together with hardware, any such effort is fundamentally limited.

**USE AT YOUR OWN RISK**

[112](https://docs.rs#112)/// code.

[114](https://docs.rs#114)/// The `Choice` struct implements operators for AND, OR, XOR, and NOT, to allow
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// combining `Choice` values. These operations do not short-circuit.
[116](https://docs.rs#116)///
[117](https://docs.rs#117)/// [rust-timing-shield]:

[146](https://docs.rs#146)    ///
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    /// The intended use case for this conversion is at the _end_ of a
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    /// higher-level primitive implementation: for example, in checking a keyed
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    /// MAC, where the verification should happen in constant-time (and thus use
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    /// a `Choice`) but it is safe to return a `bool` at the end of the
[151](https://docs.rs#151)    /// verification.
[152](https://docs.rs#152)    #[inline]
[153](https://docs.rs#153)    fn from(source: Choice) -> bool {
[154](https://docs.rs#154)        debug_assert!((source.0 == 0u8) | (source.0 == 1u8));
[155](https://docs.rs#155)        source.0 != 0
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    }
[157](https://docs.rs#157)}
[158](https://docs.rs#158)

[164](https://docs.rs#164)    }

[211](https://docs.rs#211)
[212](https://docs.rs#212)/// This function is a best-effort attempt to prevent the compiler from knowing
[213](https://docs.rs#213)/// anything about the value of the returned `u8`, other than its type.
[214](https://docs.rs#214)///
[215](https://docs.rs#215)/// Because we want to support stable Rust, we don't have access to inline
[216](https://docs.rs#216)/// assembly or test::black_box, so we use the fact that volatile values will
[217](https://docs.rs#217)/// never be elided to register values.
[218](https://docs.rs#218)///
[219](https://docs.rs#219)/// Note: Rust's notion of "volatile" is subject to change over time. While this
[220](https://docs.rs#220)/// code may break in a non-destructive way in the future, “constant-time” code
[221](https://docs.rs#221)/// is a continually moving target, and this is better than doing nothing.
[222](https://docs.rs#222)#[cfg(not(feature = "core_hint_black_box"))]
[223](https://docs.rs#223)#[inline(never)]
[224](https://docs.rs#224)fn black_box<T: Copy>(input: T) -> T {
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    unsafe {
[226](https://docs.rs#226)        // Optimization barrier
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        //
[228](https://docs.rs#228)        // SAFETY:
[229](https://docs.rs#229)        //   - &input is not NULL because we own input;
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        //   - input is Copy and always live;
[231](https://docs.rs#231)        //   - input is always properly aligned.
[232](https://docs.rs#232)        core::ptr::read_volatile(&input)
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    }
[234](https://docs.rs#234)}
[235](https://docs.rs#235)
[236](https://docs.rs#236)impl From<u8> for Choice {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    #[inline]
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    fn from(input: u8) -> Choice {
[239](https://docs.rs#239)        debug_assert!((input == 0u8) | (input == 1u8));
[240](https://docs.rs#240)
[241](https://docs.rs#241)        // Our goal is to prevent the compiler from inferring that the value held inside the
[242](https://docs.rs#242)        // resulting `Choice` struct is really a `bool` instead of a `u8`.
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        Choice(black_box(input))
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)}
[246](https://docs.rs#246)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)/// An `Eq`-like trait that produces a `Choice` instead of a `bool`.
[248](https://docs.rs#248)///
[249](https://docs.rs#249)/// # Example
[250](https://docs.rs#250)///
[251](https://docs.rs#251)/// ```
[252](https://docs.rs#252)/// use subtle::ConstantTimeEq;
[253](https://docs.rs#253)/// let x: u8 = 5;
[254](https://docs.rs#254)/// let y: u8 = 13;
[255](https://docs.rs#255)///
[256](https://docs.rs#256)/// assert_eq!(x.ct_eq(&y).unwrap_u8(), 0);
[257](https://docs.rs#257)/// assert_eq!(x.ct_eq(&x).unwrap_u8(), 1);
[258](https://docs.rs#258)/// ```
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//
[260](https://docs.rs#260)// #[inline] is specified on these function prototypes to signify that they
[261](https://docs.rs#261)#[allow(unused_attributes)] // should be in the actual implementation
[262](https://docs.rs#262)pub trait ConstantTimeEq {
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    /// Determine if two items are equal.
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    ///
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    /// The `ct_eq` function should execute in constant time.
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    ///
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    /// # Returns
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    ///
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    /// * `Choice(1u8)` if `self == other`;
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    /// * `Choice(0u8)` if `self != other`.
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    #[inline]
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    #[allow(unused_attributes)]
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    fn ct_eq(&self, other: &Self) -> Choice;
[274](https://docs.rs#274)
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    /// Determine if two items are NOT equal.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    ///
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// The `ct_ne` function should execute in constant time.
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    ///
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    /// # Returns
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    ///
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    /// * `Choice(0u8)` if `self == other`;
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    /// * `Choice(1u8)` if `self != other`.
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    #[inline]
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    fn ct_ne(&self, other: &Self) -> Choice {
[285](https://docs.rs#285)        !self.ct_eq(other)
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    }
[287](https://docs.rs#287)}
[288](https://docs.rs#288)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)impl<T: ConstantTimeEq> ConstantTimeEq for [T] {
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    /// Check whether two slices of `ConstantTimeEq` types are equal.
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    ///
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    /// # Note
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    ///
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    /// This function short-circuits if the lengths of the input slices
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    /// are different.  Otherwise, it should execute in time independent
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    /// of the slice contents.
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    ///
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    /// Since arrays coerce to slices, this function works with fixed-size arrays:
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    ///
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    /// ```
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    /// # use subtle::ConstantTimeEq;
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    /// #
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    /// let a: [u8; 8] = [0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7];
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    /// let b: [u8; 8] = [0,1,2,3,0,1,2,3];
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    ///
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    /// let a_eq_a = a.ct_eq(&a);
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    /// let a_eq_b = a.ct_eq(&b);
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    ///
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    /// assert_eq!(a_eq_a.unwrap_u8(), 1);
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    /// assert_eq!(a_eq_b.unwrap_u8(), 0);
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    /// ```
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    #[inline]
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    fn ct_eq(&self, _rhs: &[T]) -> Choice {
[314](https://docs.rs#314)        let len = self.len();
[315](https://docs.rs#315)
[316](https://docs.rs#316)        // Short-circuit on the *lengths* of the slices, not their
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        // contents.
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        if len != _rhs.len() {
[319](https://docs.rs#319)            return Choice::from(0);
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        }
[321](https://docs.rs#321)
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        // This loop shouldn't be shortcircuitable, since the compiler
[323](https://docs.rs#323)        // shouldn't be able to reason about the value of the `u8`
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        // unwrapped from the `ct_eq` result.
[325](https://docs.rs#325)        let mut x = 1u8;
[326](https://docs.rs#326)        for (ai, bi) in self.iter().zip(_rhs.iter()) {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)            x &= ai.ct_eq(bi).unwrap_u8();
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        }
[329](https://docs.rs#329)
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        x.into()
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    }
[332](https://docs.rs#332)}
[333](https://docs.rs#333)
[334](https://docs.rs#334)impl ConstantTimeEq for Choice {
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    #[inline]
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    fn ct_eq(&self, rhs: &Choice) -> Choice {
[337](https://docs.rs#337)        !(*self ^ *rhs)
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    }
[339](https://docs.rs#339)}
[340](https://docs.rs#340)
[341](https://docs.rs#341)/// Given the bit-width `$bit_width` and the corresponding primitive
[342](https://docs.rs#342)/// unsigned and signed types `$t_u` and `$t_i` respectively, generate
[343](https://docs.rs#343)/// an `ConstantTimeEq` implementation.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)macro_rules! generate_integer_equal {
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    ($t_u:ty, $t_i:ty, $bit_width:expr) => {
[346](https://docs.rs#346)        impl ConstantTimeEq for $t_u {
[347](https://docs.rs#347)            #[inline]
[348](https://docs.rs#348)            fn ct_eq(&self, other: &$t_u) -> Choice {
[349](https://docs.rs#349)                // x == 0 if and only if self == other
[350](https://docs.rs#350)                let x: $t_u = self ^ other;
[351](https://docs.rs#351)
[352](https://docs.rs#352)                // If x == 0, then x and -x are both equal to zero;
[353](https://docs.rs#353)                // otherwise, one or both will have its high bit set.
[354](https://docs.rs#354)                let y: $t_u = (x | x.wrapping_neg()) >> ($bit_width - 1);
[355](https://docs.rs#355)
[356](https://docs.rs#356)                // Result is the opposite of the high bit (now shifted to low).
[357](https://docs.rs#357)                ((y ^ (1 as $t_u)) as u8).into()
[358](https://docs.rs#358)            }
[359](https://docs.rs#359)        }
[360](https://docs.rs#360)        impl ConstantTimeEq for $t_i {
[361](https://docs.rs#361)            #[inline]
[362](https://docs.rs#362)            fn ct_eq(&self, other: &$t_i) -> Choice {
[363](https://docs.rs#363)                // Bitcast to unsigned and call that implementation.
[364](https://docs.rs#364)                (*self as $t_u).ct_eq(&(*other as $t_u))
[365](https://docs.rs#365)            }
[366](https://docs.rs#366)        }
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    };
[368](https://docs.rs#368)}
[369](https://docs.rs#369)
[370](https://docs.rs#370)generate_integer_equal!(u8, i8, 8);
[371](https://docs.rs#371)generate_integer_equal!(u16, i16, 16);
[372](https://docs.rs#372)generate_integer_equal!(u32, i32, 32);
[373](https://docs.rs#373)generate_integer_equal!(u64, i64, 64);
[374](https://docs.rs#374)#[cfg(feature = "i128")]
[375](https://docs.rs#375)generate_integer_equal!(u128, i128, 128);
[376](https://docs.rs#376)generate_integer_equal!(usize, isize, ::core::mem::size_of::<usize>() * 8);

[378](https://docs.rs#378)/// `Ordering` is `#[repr(i8)]` making it possible to leverage `i8::ct_eq`.
[379](https://docs.rs#379)impl ConstantTimeEq for cmp::Ordering {
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    #[inline]
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    fn ct_eq(&self, other: &Self) -> Choice {
[382](https://docs.rs#382)        (*self as i8).ct_eq(&(*other as i8))
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    }

[385](https://docs.rs#385)
[386](https://docs.rs#386)/// A type which can be conditionally selected in constant time.
[387](https://docs.rs#387)///
[388](https://docs.rs#388)/// This trait also provides generic implementations of conditional
[389](https://docs.rs#389)/// assignment and conditional swaps.
[390](https://docs.rs#390)//
[391](https://docs.rs#391)// #[inline] is specified on these function prototypes to signify that they
[392](https://docs.rs#392)#[allow(unused_attributes)] // should be in the actual implementation
[393](https://docs.rs#393)pub trait ConditionallySelectable: Copy {
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    /// Select `a` or `b` according to `choice`.
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    ///
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    /// # Returns
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    ///
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    /// * `a` if `choice == Choice(0)`;
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    /// * `b` if `choice == Choice(1)`.
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    ///
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    /// This function should execute in constant time.
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    ///
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    /// # Example
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    ///
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    /// ```
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    /// use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    /// #
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    /// # fn main() {
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    /// let x: u8 = 13;
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// let y: u8 = 42;
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    ///
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    /// let z = u8::conditional_select(&x, &y, 0.into());
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    /// assert_eq!(z, x);
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    /// let z = u8::conditional_select(&x, &y, 1.into());
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    /// assert_eq!(z, y);
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    /// # }
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    /// ```
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    #[inline]
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    #[allow(unused_attributes)]
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    fn conditional_select(a: &Self, b: &Self, choice: Choice) -> Self;
[421](https://docs.rs#421)
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    /// Conditionally assign `other` to `self`, according to `choice`.
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    ///
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    /// This function should execute in constant time.
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    ///
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    /// # Example
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    ///
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// ```
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    /// use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    /// #
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    /// # fn main() {
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    /// let mut x: u8 = 13;
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    /// let mut y: u8 = 42;
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    ///
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    /// x.conditional_assign(&y, 0.into());
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    /// assert_eq!(x, 13);
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    /// x.conditional_assign(&y, 1.into());
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// assert_eq!(x, 42);
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    /// # }
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    /// ```
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    #[inline]
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    fn conditional_assign(&mut self, other: &Self, choice: Choice) {
[443](https://docs.rs#443)        *self = Self::conditional_select(self, other, choice);
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    }
[445](https://docs.rs#445)
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    /// Conditionally swap `self` and `other` if `choice == 1`; otherwise,
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    /// reassign both unto themselves.
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    ///
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    /// This function should execute in constant time.
[450](https://docs.rs#450)    ///
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    /// # Example
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    ///
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    /// ```
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    /// use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    /// #
[456](https://docs.rs#456)    /// # fn main() {
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    /// let mut x: u8 = 13;
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    /// let mut y: u8 = 42;
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    ///
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    /// u8::conditional_swap(&mut x, &mut y, 0.into());
[461](https://docs.rs#461)    /// assert_eq!(x, 13);
[462](https://docs.rs#462)    /// assert_eq!(y, 42);
[463](https://docs.rs#463)    /// u8::conditional_swap(&mut x, &mut y, 1.into());
[464](https://docs.rs#464)    /// assert_eq!(x, 42);
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    /// assert_eq!(y, 13);
[466](https://docs.rs#466)    /// # }
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    /// ```
[468](https://docs.rs#468)    #[inline]
[469](https://docs.rs#469)    fn conditional_swap(a: &mut Self, b: &mut Self, choice: Choice) {
[470](https://docs.rs#470)        let t: Self = *a;
[471](https://docs.rs#471)        a.conditional_assign(&b, choice);
[472](https://docs.rs#472)        b.conditional_assign(&t, choice);
[473](https://docs.rs#473)    }

[476](https://docs.rs#476)macro_rules! to_signed_int {

[480](https://docs.rs#480)    (u16) => {
[481](https://docs.rs#481)        i16

[483](https://docs.rs#483)    (u32) => {
[484](https://docs.rs#484)        i32

[508](https://docs.rs#508)
[509](https://docs.rs#509)macro_rules! generate_integer_conditional_select {
[510](https://docs.rs#510)    ($($t:tt)*) => ($(
[511](https://docs.rs#511)        impl ConditionallySelectable for $t {
[512](https://docs.rs#512)            #[inline]
[513](https://docs.rs#513)            fn conditional_select(a: &Self, b: &Self, choice: Choice) -> Self {
[514](https://docs.rs#514)                // if choice = 0, mask = (-0) = 0000...0000
[515](https://docs.rs#515)                // if choice = 1, mask = (-1) = 1111...1111
[516](https://docs.rs#516)                let mask = -(choice.unwrap_u8() as to_signed_int!($t)) as $t;
[517](https://docs.rs#517)                a ^ (mask & (a ^ b))
[518](https://docs.rs#518)            }
[519](https://docs.rs#519)
[520](https://docs.rs#520)            #[inline]
[521](https://docs.rs#521)            fn conditional_assign(&mut self, other: &Self, choice: Choice) {
[522](https://docs.rs#522)                // if choice = 0, mask = (-0) = 0000...0000
[523](https://docs.rs#523)                // if choice = 1, mask = (-1) = 1111...1111
[524](https://docs.rs#524)                let mask = -(choice.unwrap_u8() as to_signed_int!($t)) as $t;
[525](https://docs.rs#525)                *self ^= mask & (*self ^ *other);
[526](https://docs.rs#526)            }
[527](https://docs.rs#527)
[528](https://docs.rs#528)            #[inline]
[529](https://docs.rs#529)            fn conditional_swap(a: &mut Self, b: &mut Self, choice: Choice) {
[530](https://docs.rs#530)                // if choice = 0, mask = (-0) = 0000...0000
[531](https://docs.rs#531)                // if choice = 1, mask = (-1) = 1111...1111
[532](https://docs.rs#532)                let mask = -(choice.unwrap_u8() as to_signed_int!($t)) as $t;
[533](https://docs.rs#533)                let t = mask & (*a ^ *b);
[534](https://docs.rs#534)                *a ^= t;
[535](https://docs.rs#535)                *b ^= t;
[536](https://docs.rs#536)            }
[537](https://docs.rs#537)         }
[538](https://docs.rs#538)    )*)
[539](https://docs.rs#539)}

[548](https://docs.rs#548)/// `Ordering` is `#[repr(i8)]` where:
[549](https://docs.rs#549)///
[550](https://docs.rs#550)/// - `Less` => -1
[551](https://docs.rs#551)/// - `Equal` => 0
[552](https://docs.rs#552)/// - `Greater` => 1

[559](https://docs.rs#559)        let b = *b as i8;
[560](https://docs.rs#560)        let ret = i8::conditional_select(&a, &b, choice);

[563](https://docs.rs#563)        // a value which was originally a valid `Ordering` then cast to `i8`
[564](https://docs.rs#564)        unsafe { *((&ret as *const _) as *const cmp::Ordering) }
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    }

[627](https://docs.rs#627)/// The `CtOption<T>` type represents an optional value similar to the
[628](https://docs.rs#628)/// [`Option<T>`](core::option::Option) type but is intended for
[629](https://docs.rs#629)/// use in constant time APIs.
[630](https://docs.rs#630)///
[631](https://docs.rs#631)/// Any given `CtOption<T>` is either `Some` or `None`, but unlike
[632](https://docs.rs#632)/// `Option<T>` these variants are not exposed. The
[633](https://docs.rs#633)/// [`is_some()`](CtOption::is_some) method is used to determine if
[634](https://docs.rs#634)/// the value is `Some`, and [`unwrap_or()`](CtOption::unwrap_or) and
[635](https://docs.rs#635)/// [`unwrap_or_else()`](CtOption::unwrap_or_else) methods are
[636](https://docs.rs#636)/// provided to access the underlying value. The value can also be
[637](https://docs.rs#637)/// obtained with [`unwrap()`](CtOption::unwrap) but this will panic
[638](https://docs.rs#638)/// if it is `None`.
[639](https://docs.rs#639)///
[640](https://docs.rs#640)/// Functions that are intended to be constant time may not produce
[641](https://docs.rs#641)/// valid results for all inputs, such as square root and inversion
[642](https://docs.rs#642)/// operations in finite field arithmetic. Returning an `Option<T>`
[643](https://docs.rs#643)/// from these functions makes it difficult for the caller to reason
[644](https://docs.rs#644)/// about the result in constant time, and returning an incorrect
[645](https://docs.rs#645)/// value burdens the caller and increases the chance of bugs.
[646](https://docs.rs#646)#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
[647](https://docs.rs#647)pub struct CtOption<T> {
[648](https://docs.rs#648)    value: T,
[649](https://docs.rs#649)    is_some: Choice,
[650](https://docs.rs#650)}
[651](https://docs.rs#651)
[652](https://docs.rs#652)impl<T> From<CtOption<T>> for Option<T> {
[653](https://docs.rs#653)    /// Convert the `CtOption<T>` wrapper into an `Option<T>`, depending on whether
[654](https://docs.rs#654)    /// the underlying `is_some` `Choice` was a `0` or a `1` once unwrapped.
[655](https://docs.rs#655)    ///
[656](https://docs.rs#656)    /// # Note
[657](https://docs.rs#657)    ///
[658](https://docs.rs#658)    /// This function exists to avoid ending up with ugly, verbose and/or bad handled
[659](https://docs.rs#659)    /// conversions from the `CtOption<T>` wraps to an `Option<T>` or `Result<T, E>`.
[660](https://docs.rs#660)    /// This implementation doesn't intend to be constant-time nor try to protect the
[661](https://docs.rs#661)    /// leakage of the `T` since the `Option<T>` will do it anyways.
[662](https://docs.rs#662)    fn from(source: CtOption<T>) -> Option<T> {
[663](https://docs.rs#663)        if source.is_some().unwrap_u8() == 1u8 {
[664](https://docs.rs#664)            Option::Some(source.value)
[665](https://docs.rs#665)        } else {
[666](https://docs.rs#666)            None
[667](https://docs.rs#667)        }
[668](https://docs.rs#668)    }
[669](https://docs.rs#669)}

[841](https://docs.rs#841)/// A type which can be compared in some manner and be determined to be greater
[842](https://docs.rs#842)/// than another of the same type.
[843](https://docs.rs#843)pub trait ConstantTimeGreater {
[844](https://docs.rs#844)    /// Determine whether `self > other`.
[845](https://docs.rs#845)    ///
[846](https://docs.rs#846)    /// The bitwise-NOT of the return value of this function should be usable to
[847](https://docs.rs#847)    /// determine if `self <= other`.
[848](https://docs.rs#848)    ///
[849](https://docs.rs#849)    /// This function should execute in constant time.
[850](https://docs.rs#850)    ///
[851](https://docs.rs#851)    /// # Returns
[852](https://docs.rs#852)    ///
[853](https://docs.rs#853)    /// A `Choice` with a set bit if `self > other`, and with no set bits
[854](https://docs.rs#854)    /// otherwise.
[855](https://docs.rs#855)    ///
[856](https://docs.rs#856)    /// # Example
[857](https://docs.rs#857)    ///
[858](https://docs.rs#858)    /// ```
[859](https://docs.rs#859)    /// use subtle::ConstantTimeGreater;
[860](https://docs.rs#860)    ///
[861](https://docs.rs#861)    /// let x: u8 = 13;
[862](https://docs.rs#862)    /// let y: u8 = 42;
[863](https://docs.rs#863)    ///
[864](https://docs.rs#864)    /// let x_gt_y = x.ct_gt(&y);
[865](https://docs.rs#865)    ///
[866](https://docs.rs#866)    /// assert_eq!(x_gt_y.unwrap_u8(), 0);
[867](https://docs.rs#867)    ///
[868](https://docs.rs#868)    /// let y_gt_x = y.ct_gt(&x);
[869](https://docs.rs#869)    ///
[870](https://docs.rs#870)    /// assert_eq!(y_gt_x.unwrap_u8(), 1);
[871](https://docs.rs#871)    ///
[872](https://docs.rs#872)    /// let x_gt_x = x.ct_gt(&x);
[873](https://docs.rs#873)    ///
[874](https://docs.rs#874)    /// assert_eq!(x_gt_x.unwrap_u8(), 0);
[875](https://docs.rs#875)    /// ```
[876](https://docs.rs#876)    fn ct_gt(&self, other: &Self) -> Choice;
[877](https://docs.rs#877)}
[878](https://docs.rs#878)
[879](https://docs.rs#879)macro_rules! generate_unsigned_integer_greater {
[880](https://docs.rs#880)    ($t_u: ty, $bit_width: expr) => {
[881](https://docs.rs#881)        impl ConstantTimeGreater for $t_u {
[882](https://docs.rs#882)            /// Returns Choice::from(1) iff x > y, and Choice::from(0) iff x <= y.
[883](https://docs.rs#883)            ///
[884](https://docs.rs#884)            /// # Note
[885](https://docs.rs#885)            ///
[886](https://docs.rs#886)            /// This algoritm would also work for signed integers if we first
[887](https://docs.rs#887)            /// flip the top bit, e.g. `let x: u8 = x ^ 0x80`, etc.
[888](https://docs.rs#888)            #[inline]
[889](https://docs.rs#889)            fn ct_gt(&self, other: &$t_u) -> Choice {
[890](https://docs.rs#890)                let gtb = self & !other; // All the bits in self that are greater than their corresponding bits in other.
[891](https://docs.rs#891)                let mut ltb = !self & other; // All the bits in self that are less than their corresponding bits in other.
[892](https://docs.rs#892)                let mut pow = 1;
[893](https://docs.rs#893)
[894](https://docs.rs#894)                // Less-than operator is okay here because it's dependent on the bit-width.
[895](https://docs.rs#895)                while pow < $bit_width {
[896](https://docs.rs#896)                    ltb |= ltb >> pow; // Bit-smear the highest set bit to the right.
[897](https://docs.rs#897)                    pow += pow;
[898](https://docs.rs#898)                }
[899](https://docs.rs#899)                let mut bit = gtb & !ltb; // Select the highest set bit.
[900](https://docs.rs#900)                let mut pow = 1;
[901](https://docs.rs#901)
[902](https://docs.rs#902)                while pow < $bit_width {
[903](https://docs.rs#903)                    bit |= bit >> pow; // Shift it to the right until we end up with either 0 or 1.
[904](https://docs.rs#904)                    pow += pow;
[905](https://docs.rs#905)                }
[906](https://docs.rs#906)                // XXX We should possibly do the above flattening to 0 or 1 in the
[907](https://docs.rs#907)                //     Choice constructor rather than making it a debug error?
[908](https://docs.rs#908)                Choice::from((bit & 1) as u8)
[909](https://docs.rs#909)            }
[910](https://docs.rs#910)        }
[911](https://docs.rs#911)    };
[912](https://docs.rs#912)}

# Choice in subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/subtle/2.6.1/subtle/struct.Choice.html

`pub struct Choice(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

The `Choice` struct represents a choice for use in conditional assignment.

It is a wrapper around a `u8`, which should have the value either `1` (true)
or `0` (false).

The conversion from `u8` to `Choice` passes the value through an optimization
barrier, as a best-effort attempt to prevent the compiler from inferring that
the `Choice` value is a boolean. This strategy is based on Tim Maclean’s
[work on  rust-timing-shield](https://www.chosenplaintext.ca/open-source/rust-timing-shield/security), which attempts to provide
a more comprehensive approach for preventing software side-channels in Rust
code.

The `Choice` struct implements operators for AND, OR, XOR, and NOT, to allow
combining `Choice` values. These operations do not short-circuit.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#568-573)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-ConditionallySelectable-for-Choice)### impl [ConditionallySelectable](https://docs.rs/trait.ConditionallySelectable.html) for [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#568-573)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-ConditionallySelectable-for-Choice)

### impl [ConditionallySelectable](https://docs.rs/trait.ConditionallySelectable.html) for [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/subtle/lib.rs.html#119)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Copy-for-Choice)

Convert the `Choice` wrapper into a `bool`, depending on whether
the underlying `u8` was a `0` or a `1`.

[§](https://docs.rs#note-1)Note

This function exists to avoid having higher-level cryptographic protocol implementations duplicating this pattern.

The intended use case for this conversion is at the *end* of a
higher-level primitive implementation: for example, in checking a keyed
MAC, where the verification should happen in constant-time (and thus use
a `Choice`) but it is safe to return a `bool` at the end of the
verification.

# CtOption in subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/subtle/2.6.1/subtle/struct.CtOption.html

`pub struct CtOption<T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `CtOption<T>` type represents an optional value similar to the
[ Option<T>](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html) type but is intended for
use in constant time APIs.

Any given `CtOption<T>` is either `Some` or `None`, but unlike
`Option<T>` these variants are not exposed. The
[ is_some()](https://docs.rs/struct.CtOption.html#method.is_some) method is used to determine if
the value is

`Some`, and [and](https://docs.rs/struct.CtOption.html#method.unwrap_or)

`unwrap_or()`[methods are provided to access the underlying value. The value can also be obtained with](https://docs.rs/struct.CtOption.html#method.unwrap_or_else)

`unwrap_or_else()`[but this will panic if it is](https://docs.rs/struct.CtOption.html#method.unwrap)

`unwrap()``None`.Functions that are intended to be constant time may not produce
valid results for all inputs, such as square root and inversion
operations in finite field arithmetic. Returning an `Option<T>`
from these functions makes it difficult for the caller to reason
about the result in constant time, and returning an incorrect
value burdens the caller and increases the chance of bugs.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

This method is used to construct a new `CtOption<T>` and takes
a value of type `T`, and a `Choice` that determines whether
the optional value should be `Some` or not. If `is_some` is
false, the value will still be stored but its value is never
exposed.

This returns the underlying value if it is `Some`
or the provided value otherwise.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

This function exists to avoid ending up with ugly, verbose and/or bad handled
conversions from the `CtOption<T>` wraps to an `Option<T>` or `Result<T, E>`.
This implementation doesn’t intend to be constant-time nor try to protect the
leakage of the `T` since the `Option<T>` will do it anyways.

It’s equivalent to the corresponding `From` impl, however this version is
friendlier for type inference.

#### fn [conditional_select](https://docs.rs#tymethod.conditional_select)(a: &Self, b: &Self, choice: [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html)) -> Self

Select `a` or `b` according to `choice`.

[§](https://docs.rs#returns)Returns

- `a`if- `choice == Choice(0)`;
- `b`if- `choice == Choice(1)`.

This function should execute in constant time.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
let x: u8 = 13;
let y: u8 = 42;
let z = u8::conditional_select(&x, &y, 0.into());
assert_eq!(z, x);
let z = u8::conditional_select(&x, &y, 1.into());
assert_eq!(z, y);
```

### impl [ConditionallySelectable](https://docs.rs/trait.ConditionallySelectable.html) for [Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)

`Ordering` is `#[repr(i8)]` where:

- `Less`=> -1
- `Equal`=> 0
- `Greater`=> 1

Given this, it’s possible to operate on orderings as if they’re integers, which allows leveraging conditional masking for predication.

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-ConstantTimeEq-for-%5BT%5D)

### impl<T: [ConstantTimeEq](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html)> [ConstantTimeEq](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html) for [[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)

Check whether two slices of `ConstantTimeEq` types are equal.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

This function short-circuits if the lengths of the input slices are different. Otherwise, it should execute in time independent of the slice contents.

Since arrays coerce to slices, this function works with fixed-size arrays:

```
let a: [u8; 8] = [0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7];
let b: [u8; 8] = [0,1,2,3,0,1,2,3];
let a_eq_a = a.ct_eq(&a);
let a_eq_b = a.ct_eq(&b);
assert_eq!(a_eq_a.unwrap_u8(), 1);
assert_eq!(a_eq_b.unwrap_u8(), 0);
```

# ConstantTimeLess in subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/subtle/2.6.1/subtle/trait.ConstantTimeLess.html

`pub trait ConstantTimeLess: `[ConstantTimeEq](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html) + [ConstantTimeGreater](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeGreater.html) {
    // Provided method
    fn [ct_lt](https://docs.rs#method.ct_lt)(&self, other: &Self) -> [Choice](https://docs.rs/struct.Choice.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

A type which can be compared in some manner and be determined to be less than another of the same type.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Determine whether `self < other`.

The bitwise-NOT of the return value of this function should be usable to
determine if `self >= other`.

A default implementation is provided and implemented for the unsigned integer types.

This function should execute in constant time.

[§](https://docs.rs#returns)Returns

A `Choice` with a set bit if `self < other`, and with no set bits
otherwise.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use subtle::ConstantTimeLess;
let x: u8 = 13;
let y: u8 = 42;
let x_lt_y = x.ct_lt(&y);
assert_eq!(x_lt_y.unwrap_u8(), 1);
let y_lt_x = y.ct_lt(&x);
assert_eq!(y_lt_x.unwrap_u8(), 0);
let x_lt_x = x.ct_lt(&x);
assert_eq!(x_lt_x.unwrap_u8(), 0);
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

# subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/subtle/latest/subtle/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#subtle---)subtle

**Pure-Rust traits and utilities for constant-time cryptographic implementations.**

It consists of a `Choice` type, and a collection of traits using `Choice`
instead of `bool` which are intended to execute in constant-time.  The `Choice`
type is a wrapper around a `u8` that holds a `0` or `1`.

`subtle = "2.6"`This crate represents a “best-effort” attempt, since side-channels are ultimately a property of a deployed cryptographic system including the hardware it runs on, not just of software.

The traits are implemented using bitwise operations, and should execute in constant time provided that a) the bitwise operations are constant-time and b) the bitwise operations are not recognized as a conditional assignment and optimized back into a branch.

For a compiler to recognize that bitwise operations represent a conditional
assignment, it needs to know that the value used to generate the bitmasks is
really a boolean `i1` rather than an `i8` byte value. In an attempt to
prevent this refinement, the crate tries to hide the value of a `Choice`’s
inner `u8` by passing it through a volatile read. For more information, see
the *About* section below.

Rust versions from 1.51 or higher have const generics support. You may enable
`const-generics` feautre to have `subtle` traits implemented for arrays `[T; N]`.

Versions prior to `2.2` recommended use of the `nightly` feature to enable an
optimization barrier; this is not required in versions `2.2` and above.

Note: the `subtle` crate contains `debug_assert`s to check invariants during
debug builds. These invariant checks involve secret-dependent branches, and
are not present when compiled in release mode. This crate is intended to be
used in release mode.

- Wrapper type which implements an optimization barrier for all accesses.

- The `Choice`struct represents a choice for use in conditional assignment.

- The `CtOption<T>`type represents an optional value similar to the`Option<T>`

- A type which can be conditionally negated in constant time.
- [Conditionally](https://docs.rs/trait.ConditionallySelectable.html)- Selectable
- A type which can be conditionally selected in constant time.
- [Constant](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html)- Time - Eq
- An `Eq`-like trait that produces a`Choice`instead of a`bool`.
- [Constant](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeGreater.html)- Time - Greater
- A type which can be compared in some manner and be determined to be greater than another of the same type.
- [Constant](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstantTimeLess.html)- Time - Less
- A type which can be compared in some manner and be determined to be less than another of the same type.

# rand 0.8.6 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand/^0.8

# Rand

A Rust library for random number generation, featuring:

- Easy random value generation and usage via the `Rng``SliceRandom``IteratorRandom`
- Secure seeding via the `getrandom`crate`thread_rng`
- A modular design built over `rand_core`[see the book](https://rust-random.github.io/book/crates.html))
- Fast implementations of the best-in-class [cryptographic](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#cryptographically-secure-pseudo-random-number-generators-csprngs)and[non-cryptographic](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#basic-pseudo-random-number-generators-prngs)generators
- A flexible `distributions`
- Samplers for a large number of random number distributions via our own
`rand_distr``statrs`
- [Portably reproducible output](https://rust-random.github.io/book/portability.html)
- `#[no_std]`compatibility (partial)
- *Many*performance optimisations

It's also worth pointing out what `rand` *is not*:

- Small. Most low-level crates are small, but the higher-level `rand`and`rand_distr`each contain a lot of functionality.
- Simple (implementation). We have a strong focus on correctness, speed and flexibility, but
not simplicity. If you prefer a small-and-simple library, there are
alternatives including [fastrand](https://crates.io/crates/fastrand)and[oorandom](https://crates.io/crates/oorandom).
- Slow. We take performance seriously, with considerations also for set-up time of new distributions, commonly-used parameters, and parameters of the current sampler.

Documentation:

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.8.4"
```
To get started using Rand, see [The Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

## Versions

Rand is *mature* (suitable for general usage, with infrequent breaking releases
which minimise breakage) but not yet at 1.0. We maintain compatibility with
pinned versions of the Rust compiler (see below).

Current Rand versions are:

- Version 0.7 was released in June 2019, moving most non-uniform distributions
to an external crate, moving `from_entropy`to`SeedableRng`, and many small changes and fixes.
- Version 0.8 was released in December 2020 with many small changes.

A detailed [changelog](https://docs.rs/CHANGELOG.md) is available for releases.

When upgrading to the next minor series (especially 0.4 → 0.5), we recommend
reading the [Upgrade Guide](https://rust-random.github.io/book/update.html).

Rand has not yet reached 1.0 implying some breaking changes may arrive in the
future ([SemVer](https://semver.org/) allows each 0.x.0 release to include
breaking changes), but is considered *mature*: breaking changes are minimised
and breaking releases are infrequent.

Rand libs have inter-dependencies and make use of the
[semver trick](https://github.com/dtolnay/semver-trick/) in order to make traits
compatible across crate versions. (This is especially important for `RngCore`
and `SeedableRng`.) A few crate releases are thus compatibility shims,
depending on the *next* lib version (e.g. `rand_core` versions `0.2.2` and
`0.3.1`). This means, for example, that `rand_core_0_4_0::SeedableRng` and
`rand_core_0_3_0::SeedableRng` are distinct, incompatible traits, which can
cause build errors. Usually, running `cargo update` is enough to fix any issues.

### Yanked versions

Some versions of Rand crates have been yanked ("unreleased"). Where this occurs,
the crate's CHANGELOG *should* be updated with a rationale, and a search on the
issue tracker with the keyword `yank` *should* uncover the motivation.

### Rust version requirements

Since version 0.8, Rand requires **Rustc version 1.36 or greater**.
Rand 0.7 requires Rustc 1.32 or greater while versions 0.5 require Rustc 1.22 or
greater, and 0.4 and 0.3 (since approx. June 2017) require Rustc version 1.15 or
greater. Subsets of the Rand code may work with older Rust versions, but this is
not supported.

Continuous Integration (CI) will always test the minimum supported Rustc version (the MSRV). The current policy is that this can be updated in any Rand release if required, but the change must be noted in the changelog.

## Crate Features

Rand is built with these features enabled by default:

- `std`enables functionality dependent on the- `std`lib
- `alloc`(implied by- `std`) enables functionality requiring an allocator
- `getrandom`(implied by- `std`) is an optional dependency providing the code behind- `rngs::OsRng`
- `std_rng`enables inclusion of- `StdRng`,- `thread_rng`and- `random`(the latter two- *also*require that- `std`be enabled)

Additionally, these features configure Rand:

- `small_rng`enables inclusion of the- `SmallRng`PRNG
- `nightly`enables some optimizations requiring nightly Rust
- `min_const_gen`enables generating random arrays of any size using min-const-generics, requiring Rust ≥ 1.51.

Note that nightly features are not stable and therefore not all library and
compiler versions will be compatible. This is especially true of Rand's
experimental `simd_support` feature, which was dropped by version 0.8.6 of Rand.

Rand supports limited functionality in `no_std` mode (enabled via
`default-features = false`). In this case, `OsRng` and `from_entropy` are
unavailable (unless `getrandom` is enabled), large parts of `seq` are
unavailable (unless `alloc` is enabled), and `thread_rng` and `random` are
unavailable.

### WASM support

The WASM target `wasm32-unknown-unknown` is not *automatically* supported by
`rand` or `getrandom`. To solve this, either use a different target such as
`wasm32-wasi` or add a direct dependency on `getrandom` with the `js` feature
(if the target supports JavaScript). See
[getrandom#WebAssembly support](https://docs.rs/getrandom/latest/getrandom/#webassembly-support).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://docs.rs/COPYRIGHT) for details.

# subtle 2.6.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/subtle/2.6.0

**Pure-Rust traits and utilities for constant-time cryptographic implementations.**

It consists of a `Choice` type, and a collection of traits using `Choice`
instead of `bool` which are intended to execute in constant-time.  The `Choice`
type is a wrapper around a `u8` that holds a `0` or `1`.

```
 = "2.6"
```
This crate represents a “best-effort” attempt, since side-channels are ultimately a property of a deployed cryptographic system including the hardware it runs on, not just of software.

The traits are implemented using bitwise operations, and should execute in constant time provided that a) the bitwise operations are constant-time and b) the bitwise operations are not recognized as a conditional assignment and optimized back into a branch.

For a compiler to recognize that bitwise operations represent a conditional
assignment, it needs to know that the value used to generate the bitmasks is
really a boolean `i1` rather than an `i8` byte value. In an attempt to
prevent this refinement, the crate tries to hide the value of a `Choice`'s
inner `u8` by passing it through a volatile read. For more information, see
the *About* section below.

Rust versions from 1.51 or higher have const generics support. You may enable
`const-generics` feautre to have `subtle` traits implemented for arrays `[T; N]`.

Versions prior to `2.2` recommended use of the `nightly` feature to enable an
optimization barrier; this is not required in versions `2.2` and above.

Note: the `subtle` crate contains `debug_assert`s to check invariants during
debug builds. These invariant checks involve secret-dependent branches, and
are not present when compiled in release mode. This crate is intended to be
used in release mode.

## Documentation

Documentation is available [here](https://docs.rs/subtle).

## Minimum Supported Rust Version

Rust **1.41** or higher.

Minimum supported Rust version can be changed in the future, but it will be done with a minor version bump.

## About

This library aims to be the Rust equivalent of Go’s `crypto/subtle` module.

Old versions of the optimization barrier in `impl From<u8> for Choice` were
based on Tim Maclean's [work on  rust-timing-shield](https://www.chosenplaintext.ca/open-source/rust-timing-shield/security),
which attempts to provide a more comprehensive approach for preventing
software side-channels in Rust code.
From version

`2.2`, it was based on Diane Hosfelt and Amber Sprenkels' work on
"Secret Types in Rust".`subtle` is authored by isis agora lovecruft and Henry de Valence.

## Warning

This code is a low-level library, intended for specific use-cases implementing cryptographic protocols. It represents a best-effort attempt to protect against some software side-channels. Because side-channel resistance is not a property of software alone, but of software together with hardware, any such effort is fundamentally limited.

**USE AT YOUR OWN RISK**

type is a wrapper around a `u8` that holds a `0` or `1`.

The traits are implemented using bitwise operations, and should execute in constant time provided that a) the bitwise operations are constant-time and b) the operations are not optimized into a branch.

To prevent the latter possibility, when using the `nightly` feature
(recommended), the crate attempts to hide the value of a `Choice`'s inner `u8`
from the optimizer, by passing it through an inline assembly block.  For more
information, see the *About* section below.

```
[]
 = "2.1"
 = ["nightly"]
```
## Features

- The `nightly`feature enables the use of an optimization barrier to protect the`Choice`type.*Using the*.`nightly`feature is recommended for security

## Documentation

Documentation is available [here](https://doc.dalek.rs/subtle).

## About

This library aims to be the Rust equivalent of Go’s `crypto/subtle` module.

The optimization barrier in `impl From<u8> for Choice` was based on Tim
Maclean's [work on  rust-timing-shield](https://www.chosenplaintext.ca/open-source/rust-timing-shield/security), which attempts to
provide a more comprehensive approach for preventing software side-channels in
Rust code.

`subtle` is authored by isis agora lovecruft and Henry de Valence.

## Warning

This code is a low-level library, intended for specific use-cases implementing cryptographic protocols. It represents a best-effort attempt to protect against some software side-channels. Because side-channel resistance is not a property of software alone, but of software together with hardware, any such effort is fundamentally limited.

**USE AT YOUR OWN RISK**

**Pure-Rust traits and utilities for constant-time cryptographic implementations.**

This crate represents a "best-effort" attempt, since side-channels are ultimately a property of a deployed cryptographic system including the hardware it runs on, not just of software.

The `nightly`feature enables`u128`/`i128`support and the use of the`test::black_box`optimization barrier to protect the`Choice`type.
-
The `generic-impls`feature (enabled by default) provides generic impls of some traits. It can be disabled to allow specialized impls without impl conflicts.

## Documentation

Documentation is available [here](https://docs.rs/subtle).

## About

Significant portions of this code were based upon Golang's "crypto/subtle" module, and this library aims to be that library's Rust equivalent.

## Warning

This code has **not** yet received sufficient peer review by other qualified
cryptographers to be considered in any way, shape, or form, safe.  Further, this
library does **not** provide much in the way of assurance against deliberate
misuse.  Instead, it is a low-level library, mostly of bit-flipping tricks,
intended for other cryptographers who would like to implement their own
constant-time libraries.  (For an example usage of this library, please see
[curve25519-dalek](https://github.com/dalek-cryptography/curve25519-dalek) and
[ed25519-dalek](https://github.com/dalek-cryptography/ed25519-dalek).)

# subtle 0.6.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/subtle/0.6.0

**Pure-Rust traits and utilities for constant-time cryptographic implementations.**

This crate represents a "best-effort" attempt, since side-channels are ultimately a property of a deployed cryptographic system including the hardware it runs on, not just of software.

It consists of a `Choice` type, a wrapper around a `u8` that holds a
`0` or `1`, and a collection of traits using `Choice` instead of
`bool`.  Implementations of these traits are provided for primitive
types.

```
[]
 = "^0.6"
 = ["nightly"]
```
## Features

-
The `nightly`feature enables`u128`/`i128`support and the use of the`test::black_box`optimization barrier to protect the`Choice`type.
-
The `generic-impls`feature (enabled by default) provides generic impls of some traits. It can be disabled to allow specialized impls without impl conflicts.

## Documentation
