# subtle 0.5.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/subtle/0.5.1

**Pure-Rust traits and utilities for constant-time cryptographic implementations.**

Significant portions of this code are based upon Golang's "crypto/subtle" module, and this library aims to be that library's Rust equivalent¹, plus more.

¹ The only function in Golang's "crypto/subtle" module which we do not implement
is `ConstantTimeLessOrEq`.  This is for two reasons: first, that
`ConstantTimeLessOrEq`, as far as this author knows, is only used to implement
the RSA encryption padding scheme defined in the (now outdated) PKCS#1 v1.5
standard (superseded by the newer RSA-OAEP mode).  Not only should use of this
outdated mode cease to continue, it is known to be dangerous for encrypting
anything other than a symmetric session key.  Second, without other constant-time
comparison functions (e.g. "greater or equal"), this author feels that
providing solely `ConstantTimeLessOrEq` would provide a
weird/incomplete API.

## Warning

This code has **not** yet received sufficient peer review by other qualified
cryptographers to be considered in any way, shape, or form, safe.  Further, this
library does **not** provide much in the way of assurance against deliberate
misuse.  Instead, it is a low-level library, mostly of bit-flipping tricks,
intended for other cryptographers who would like to implement their own
constant-time libraries.  (For an example usage of this library, please see
[curve25519-dalek](https://github.com/dalek-cryptography/curve25519-dalek) and
[ed25519-dalek](https://github.com/dalek-cryptography/ed25519-dalek).)

**USE AT YOUR OWN RISK**

## Documentation

Extensive documentation is available [here](https://docs.rs/subtle).

`Cargo.toml`:

```

```

# subtle 2.6.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/subtle/latest/source/CHANGELOG.md

#Changelog
Entries are listed in reverse chronological order.
##2.5.0*Add constant-timedness note to the documentation for `CtOption::unwrap_or_else`.
* Add `CtOption::expect`.
* Add `ConstantTimeEq::ct_ne` with default implementation.
* Add new `core_hint_black_box` feature from Diane Hosfelt and Amber
Sprenkels which utilises the original `black_box` functionality from
when subtle was first written, which has now found it's way into the
Rust standard library.
* Add new `const-generics` feature from @survived which adds support
for subtle traits for generic arrays `[T; N]`.
* Add new feature for supporting `core::cmp::Ordering` for types which
implement subtle traits, patch from @tarcieri.
* Update `rand` dependency to 0.8.
##2.4.1*Fix a bug in how the README was included in the documentation builds
which caused nightly builds to break.
##2.4.0*Add new `ConstantTimeGreater` and `ConstantTimeLess` traits, as well
as implementations for unsigned integers, by @isislovecruft.
##2.3.0*Add `impl ConstantTimeEq for Choice` by @tarcieri.
* Add `impl From<CtOption<T>> for Option<T>` by @CPerezz. This is useful for
handling library code that produces `CtOption`s in contexts where timing
doesn't matter.
* Introduce an MSRV policy.
##2.2.3*Remove the `nightly`-only asm-based `black_box` barrier in favor of the
volatile-based one, fixing compilation on current nightlies.
##2.2.2*Update README.md to clarify that 2.2 and above do not require the `nightly`feature.
##2.2.1*Adds an `or_else` combinator for `CtOption`, by @ebfull.
* Optimized `black_box` for `nightly`, by @jethrogb.
* Optimized `black_box` for `stable`, by @dsprenkels.
* Fixed CI for `no_std`, by @dsprenkels.
* Fixed fuzz target compilation, by @3for.
##2.2.0*Error during `cargo publish`, yanked.
##2.1.1*Adds the "crypto" tag to crate metadata.
* New shorter, more efficient ct_eq() for integers, contributed by Thomas Pornin.
##2.1.0*Adds a new `CtOption<T>` which acts as a constant-time `Option<T>`(thanks to @ebfull for the implementation).
*`Choice` now itself implements `ConditionallySelectable`.
##2.0.0*Stable version with traits reworked from 1.0.0 to interact better
with the orphan rules.

# subtle 2.6.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/subtle/latest/source/README.md

```
**Pure-Rust traits and utilities for constant-time cryptographic implementations.**
It consists of a `Choice` type, and a collection of traits using `Choice`
instead of `bool` which are intended to execute in constant-time.  The `Choice`
type is a wrapper around a `u8` that holds a `0` or `1`.
```toml
subtle = "2.6"
```
This crate represents a “best-effort” attempt, since side-channels
are ultimately a property of a deployed cryptographic system
including the hardware it runs on, not just of software.
The traits are implemented using bitwise operations, and should execute in
constant time provided that a) the bitwise operations are constant-time and
b) the bitwise operations are not recognized as a conditional assignment and
optimized back into a branch.
For a compiler to recognize that bitwise operations represent a conditional
assignment, it needs to know that the value used to generate the bitmasks is
really a boolean `i1` rather than an `i8` byte value. In an attempt to
prevent this refinement, the crate tries to hide the value of a `Choice`'s
inner `u8` by passing it through a volatile read. For more information, see
the _About_ section below.
Rust versions from 1.51 or higher have const generics support. You may enable
`const-generics` feautre to have `subtle` traits implemented for arrays `[T; N]`.
Versions prior to `2.2` recommended use of the `nightly` feature to enable an
optimization barrier; this is not required in versions `2.2` and above.
Note: the `subtle` crate contains `debug_assert`s to check invariants during
debug builds. These invariant checks involve secret-dependent branches, and
are not present when compiled in release mode. This crate is intended to be
used in release mode.
Documentation is available [here][docs].
Rust **1.41** or higher.
Minimum supported Rust version can be changed in the future, but it will be done with a minor version bump.
This library aims to be the Rust equivalent of Go’s `crypto/subtle` module.
Old versions of the optimization barrier in `impl From<u8> for Choice` were
based on Tim Maclean's [work on `rust-timing-shield`][rust-timing-shield],
which attempts to provide a more comprehensive approach for preventing
software side-channels in Rust code.
From version `2.2`, it was based on Diane Hosfelt and Amber Sprenkels' work on
"Secret Types in Rust".
`subtle` is authored by isis agora lovecruft and Henry de Valence.
This code is a low-level library, intended for specific use-cases implementing
cryptographic protocols.  It represents a best-effort attempt to protect
against some software side-channels.  Because side-channel resistance is not a
property of software alone, but of software together with hardware, any such
effort is fundamentally limited.
**USE AT YOUR OWN RISK**
```

---

# rand 0.8.6 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand/0.8.6

# Rand

A Rust library for random number generation, featuring:

- Easy random value generation and usage via the `Rng``SliceRandom``IteratorRandom`
- Secure seeding via the `getrandom`crate`thread_rng`
- A modular design built over `rand_core`[see the book](https://rust-random.github.io/book/crates.html))
- Fast implementations of the best-in-class [cryptographic](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#cryptographically-secure-pseudo-random-number-generators-csprngs)and[non-cryptographic](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#basic-pseudo-random-number-generators-prngs)generators
- A flexible `distributions`
- Samplers for a large number of random number distributions via our own
`rand_distr``statrs`
- [Portably reproducible output](https://rust-random.github.io/book/portability.html)
- `#[no_std]`compatibility (partial)
- *Many*performance optimisations

It's also worth pointing out what `rand` *is not*:

- Small. Most low-level crates are small, but the higher-level `rand`and`rand_distr`each contain a lot of functionality.
- Simple (implementation). We have a strong focus on correctness, speed and flexibility, but
not simplicity. If you prefer a small-and-simple library, there are
alternatives including [fastrand](https://crates.io/crates/fastrand)and[oorandom](https://crates.io/crates/oorandom).
- Slow. We take performance seriously, with considerations also for set-up time of new distributions, commonly-used parameters, and parameters of the current sampler.

Documentation:

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.8.4"
```
To get started using Rand, see [The Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

## Versions

Rand is *mature* (suitable for general usage, with infrequent breaking releases
which minimise breakage) but not yet at 1.0. We maintain compatibility with
pinned versions of the Rust compiler (see below).

Current Rand versions are:

- Version 0.7 was released in June 2019, moving most non-uniform distributions
to an external crate, moving `from_entropy`to`SeedableRng`, and many small changes and fixes.
- Version 0.8 was released in December 2020 with many small changes.

A detailed [changelog](https://docs.rs/CHANGELOG.md) is available for releases.

When upgrading to the next minor series (especially 0.4 → 0.5), we recommend
reading the [Upgrade Guide](https://rust-random.github.io/book/update.html).

Rand has not yet reached 1.0 implying some breaking changes may arrive in the
future ([SemVer](https://semver.org/) allows each 0.x.0 release to include
breaking changes), but is considered *mature*: breaking changes are minimised
and breaking releases are infrequent.

Rand libs have inter-dependencies and make use of the
[semver trick](https://github.com/dtolnay/semver-trick/) in order to make traits
compatible across crate versions. (This is especially important for `RngCore`
and `SeedableRng`.) A few crate releases are thus compatibility shims,
depending on the *next* lib version (e.g. `rand_core` versions `0.2.2` and
`0.3.1`). This means, for example, that `rand_core_0_4_0::SeedableRng` and
`rand_core_0_3_0::SeedableRng` are distinct, incompatible traits, which can
cause build errors. Usually, running `cargo update` is enough to fix any issues.

### Yanked versions

Some versions of Rand crates have been yanked ("unreleased"). Where this occurs,
the crate's CHANGELOG *should* be updated with a rationale, and a search on the
issue tracker with the keyword `yank` *should* uncover the motivation.

### Rust version requirements

Since version 0.8, Rand requires **Rustc version 1.36 or greater**.
Rand 0.7 requires Rustc 1.32 or greater while versions 0.5 require Rustc 1.22 or
greater, and 0.4 and 0.3 (since approx. June 2017) require Rustc version 1.15 or
greater. Subsets of the Rand code may work with older Rust versions, but this is
not supported.

Continuous Integration (CI) will always test the minimum supported Rustc version (the MSRV). The current policy is that this can be updated in any Rand release if required, but the change must be noted in the changelog.

## Crate Features

Rand is built with these features enabled by default:

- `std`enables functionality dependent on the- `std`lib
- `alloc`(implied by- `std`) enables functionality requiring an allocator
- `getrandom`(implied by- `std`) is an optional dependency providing the code behind- `rngs::OsRng`
- `std_rng`enables inclusion of- `StdRng`,- `thread_rng`and- `random`(the latter two- *also*require that- `std`be enabled)

Additionally, these features configure Rand:

- `small_rng`enables inclusion of the- `SmallRng`PRNG
- `nightly`enables some optimizations requiring nightly Rust
- `min_const_gen`enables generating random arrays of any size using min-const-generics, requiring Rust ≥ 1.51.

Note that nightly features are not stable and therefore not all library and
compiler versions will be compatible. This is especially true of Rand's
experimental `simd_support` feature, which was dropped by version 0.8.6 of Rand.

Rand supports limited functionality in `no_std` mode (enabled via
`default-features = false`). In this case, `OsRng` and `from_entropy` are
unavailable (unless `getrandom` is enabled), large parts of `seq` are
unavailable (unless `alloc` is enabled), and `thread_rng` and `random` are
unavailable.

### WASM support

The WASM target `wasm32-unknown-unknown` is not *automatically* supported by
`rand` or `getrandom`. To solve this, either use a different target such as
`wasm32-wasi` or add a direct dependency on `getrandom` with the `js` feature
(if the target supports JavaScript). See
[getrandom#WebAssembly support](https://docs.rs/getrandom/latest/getrandom/#webassembly-support).

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.103/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# bincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bincode/^1.2.1/

## Expand description

Bincode is a crate for encoding and decoding using a tiny binary serialization strategy. Using it, you can easily go from having an object in memory, quickly serialize it to bytes, and then deserialize it back just as fast!

[§](https://docs.rs#using-basic-functions)Using Basic Functions

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    // The object that we will serialize.
    let target: Option<String>  = Some("hello world".to_string());
    let encoded: Vec<u8> = bincode::serialize(&target).unwrap();
    let decoded: Option<String> = bincode::deserialize(&encoded[..]).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(target, decoded);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#128bit-numbers)128bit numbers

Support for `i128` and `u128` is automatically enabled on Rust toolchains
greater than or equal to `1.26.0` and disabled for targets which do not support it

# rand_pcg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_pcg/^0.3.0/

## Expand description

The PCG random number generators.

This is a native Rust implementation of a small selection of PCG generators. The primary goal of this crate is simple, minimal, well-tested code; in other words it is explicitly not a goal to re-implement all of PCG.

This crate provides:

- `Pcg32`aka- `Lcg64Xsh32`, officially known as- `pcg32`, a general purpose RNG. This is a good choice on both 32-bit and 64-bit CPUs (for 32-bit output).
- `Pcg64`aka- `Lcg128Xsl64`, officially known as- `pcg64`, a general purpose RNG. This is a good choice on 64-bit CPUs.
- `Pcg64Mcg`aka- `Mcg128Xsl64`, officially known as- `pcg64_fast`, a general purpose RNG using 128-bit multiplications. This has poor performance on 32-bit CPUs but is a good choice on 64-bit CPUs for both 32-bit and 64-bit output.

Both of these use 16 bytes of state and 128-bit seeds, and are considered value-stable (i.e. any change affecting the output given a fixed seed would be considered a breaking change to the crate).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- A PCG random number generator (XSH RR 64/32 (LCG) variant).
- A PCG random number generator (XSL RR 128/64 (LCG) variant).
- A PCG random number generator (XSL 128/64 (MCG) variant).

- The 64-bit libc on Solaris and illumos only has readdir_r. If a 32-bit Solaris or illumos target is ever created, it should use __posix_readdir_r. See libc(3LIB) on Solaris or illumos: https://illumos.org/man/3lib/libc https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E36784_01/html/E36873/libc-3lib.html https://www.unix.com/man-page/opensolaris/3LIB/libc/

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand/latest/target-redirect/rand/

## Expand description

Random-number generators and samplers

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
// rand::random() supports many common types:
println!("Uniform i8 sample: {}", match rand::random() {
    0i8 => "zero",
    i if i > 0 => "positive",
    _ => "negative",
});
// Ranged sampling:
use std::f32::consts::PI;
println!("Angle: {} degrees", rand::random_range(-PI..PI));
```
See also [The Book: Quick Start](https://rust-random.github.io/book/quick-start.html).

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand/0.8.6/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/rand/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

To get you started quickly, the easiest and highest-level way to get
a random value is to use [ random()](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html); alternatively you can use

[. The](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)

`thread_rng()`[trait provides a useful API on all RNGs, while the](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[and](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)

`distributions`[modules provide further functionality on top of RNGs.](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)

`seq````
use rand::prelude::*;
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    // Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
    println!("char: {}", rand::random::<char>());
}
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let y: f64 = rng.gen(); // generates a float between 0 and 1
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [distributions](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)
- Generating random samples from probability distributions
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Convenience re-export of common members
- [rngs](https://docs.rs/rngs/index.html)
- Random number generators and adapters
- [seq](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)
- Sequence-related functionality

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error type of random number generators

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Crypto](https://docs.rs/trait.CryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait used to indicate that an `RngCore``BlockRngCore`
- [Fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Fill.html)
- Types which may be filled with random data
- [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)
- An automatically-implemented extension trait on `RngCore`
- [RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html)
- The core of a random number generator.
- [Seedable](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html)- Rng
- A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [random](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html)- `std`and- `std_rng`
- Generates a random value using the thread-local random number generator.
- [thread_](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)- rng - `std`and- `std_rng`
- Retrieve the lazily-initialized thread-local random number generator,
seeded by the system. Intended to be used in method chaining style,
e.g. `thread_rng().gen::<i32>()`, or cached locally, e.g.`let mut rng = thread_rng();`. Invoked by the`Default`trait, making`ThreadRng::default()`equivalent.

# random in rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8/fn.random.html

`pub fn random<T>() -> T`**crate features**only.

`std` and `std_rng`## Expand description

Generates a random value using the thread-local random number generator.

This is simply a shortcut for `thread_rng().gen()`. See [ thread_rng](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html) for
documentation of the entropy source and

[for documentation of distributions and type-specific generation.](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.Standard.html)

`Standard`[§](https://docs.rs#provided-implementations)Provided implementations

The following types have provided implementations that generate values with the following ranges and distributions:

- Integers (`i32`,`u32`,`isize`,`usize`, etc.): Uniformly distributed over all values of the type.
- `char`: Uniformly distributed over all Unicode scalar values, i.e. all code points in the range- `0...0x10_FFFF`, except for the range- `0xD800...0xDFFF`(the surrogate code points). This includes unassigned/reserved code points.
- `bool`: Generates- `false`or- `true`, each with probability 0.5.
- Floating point types (`f32`and`f64`): Uniformly distributed in the half-open range`[0, 1)`. See notes below.
- Wrapping integers (`Wrapping<T>`), besides the type identical to their normal integer variants.

Also supported is the generation of the following compound types where all component types are supported:

- Tuples (up to 12 elements): each element is generated sequentially.
- Arrays (up to 32 elements): each element is generated sequentially;
see also `Rng::fill``u32`and smaller types.
- `Option<T>`first generates a- `bool`, and if true generates and returns- `Some(value)`where- `value: T`, otherwise returning- `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let x = rand::random::<u8>();
println!("{}", x);
let y = rand::random::<f64>();
println!("{}", y);
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    println!("Better lucky than good!");
}
```
If you’re calling `random()` in a loop, caching the generator as in the
following example can increase performance.

```
use rand::Rng;
let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];
for x in v.iter_mut() {
    *x = rand::random()
}
// can be made faster by caching thread_rng
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
for x in v.iter_mut() {
    *x = rng.gen();
}
```

}## Expand description

An automatically-implemented extension trait on [ RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html) providing high-level
generic methods for sampling values and other convenience methods.

This is the primary trait to use when generating random values.

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-usage)Generic usage

The basic pattern is `fn foo<R: Rng + ?Sized>(rng: &mut R)`. Some
things are worth noting here:

- Since `Rng: RngCore`and every`RngCore`implements`Rng`, it makes no difference whether we use`R: Rng`or`R: RngCore`.
- The `+ ?Sized`un-bounding allows functions to be called directly on type-erased references; i.e.`foo(r)`where`r: &mut dyn RngCore`. Without this it would be necessary to write`foo(&mut r)`.

An alternative pattern is possible: `fn foo<R: Rng>(rng: R)`. This has some
trade-offs. It allows the argument to be consumed directly without a `&mut`
(which is how `from_rng(thread_rng())` works); also it still works directly
on references (including type-erased references). Unfortunately within the
function `foo` it is not known whether `rng` is a reference type or not,
hence many uses of `rng` require an extra reference, either explicitly
(`distr.sample(&mut rng)`) or implicitly (`rng.gen()`); one may hope the
optimiser can remove redundant references later.

Example:

```
use rand::Rng;
fn foo<R: Rng + ?Sized>(rng: &mut R) -> f32 {
    rng.gen()
}
```
## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Return a random value supporting the [ Standard](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.Standard.html) distribution.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::{thread_rng, Rng};
let mut rng = thread_rng();
let x: u32 = rng.gen();
println!("{}", x);
println!("{:?}", rng.gen::<(f64, bool)>());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#arrays-and-tuples)Arrays and tuples

The `rng.gen()` method is able to generate arrays (up to 32 elements)
and tuples (up to 12 elements), so long as all element types can be
generated.
When using `rustc` ≥ 1.51, enable the `min_const_gen` feature to support
arrays larger than 32 elements.

For arrays of integers, especially for those with small element types
(< 64 bit), it will likely be faster to instead use [ Rng::fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html#method.fill).

```
use rand::{thread_rng, Rng};
let mut rng = thread_rng();
let tuple: (u8, i32, char) = rng.gen(); // arbitrary tuple support
let arr1: [f32; 32] = rng.gen();        // array construction
let mut arr2 = [0u8; 128];
rng.fill(&mut arr2);                    // array fill
```
Generate a random value in the given range.

This function is optimised for the case that only a single sample is
made from the given range. See also the [ Uniform](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.Uniform.html) distribution
type which may be faster if sampling from the same range repeatedly.

Only `gen_range(low..high)` and `gen_range(low..=high)` are supported.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the range is empty.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use rand::{thread_rng, Rng};
let mut rng = thread_rng();
// Exclusive range
let n: u32 = rng.gen_range(0..10);
println!("{}", n);
let m: f64 = rng.gen_range(-40.0..1.3e5);
println!("{}", m);
// Inclusive range
let n: u32 = rng.gen_range(0..=10);
println!("{}", n);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand/rng.rs.html#192-198)#### fn [sample_iter](https://docs.rs#method.sample_iter)<T, D>(self, distr: D) -> [DistIter](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.DistIter.html)<D, Self, T> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand/rng.rs.html#192-198)

#### fn [sample_iter](https://docs.rs#method.sample_iter)<T, D>(self, distr: D) -> [DistIter](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.DistIter.html)<D, Self, T> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

Create an iterator that generates values using the given distribution.

Note that this function takes its arguments by value. This works since
`(&mut R): Rng where R: Rng` and
`(&D): Distribution where D: Distribution`,
however borrowing is not automatic hence `rng.sample_iter(...)` may
need to be replaced with `(&mut rng).sample_iter(...)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
use rand::{thread_rng, Rng};
use rand::distributions::{Alphanumeric, Uniform, Standard};
let mut rng = thread_rng();
// Vec of 16 x f32:
let v: Vec<f32> = (&mut rng).sample_iter(Standard).take(16).collect();
// String:
let s: String = (&mut rng).sample_iter(Alphanumeric)
    .take(7)
    .map(char::from)
    .collect();
// Combined values
println!("{:?}", (&mut rng).sample_iter(Standard).take(5)
                             .collect::<Vec<(f64, bool)>>());
// Dice-rolling:
let die_range = Uniform::new_inclusive(1, 6);
let mut roll_die = (&mut rng).sample_iter(die_range);
while roll_die.next().unwrap() != 6 {
    println!("Not a 6; rolling again!");
}
```

Return a bool with a probability of `numerator/denominator` of being

returning true. If `numerator == denominator`, then the returned value

sampling from the same

# CryptoRng in rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8/trait.CryptoRng.html

`pub trait CryptoRng { }`## Expand description

A marker trait used to indicate that an [ RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html) or

[implementation is supposed to be cryptographically secure.](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.6.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/block/trait.BlockRngCore.html)

`BlockRngCore`*Cryptographically secure generators*, also known as *CSPRNGs*, should
satisfy an additional properties over other generators: given the first
*k* bits of an algorithm’s output
sequence, it should not be possible using polynomial-time algorithms to
predict the next bit with probability significantly greater than 50%.

Some generators may satisfy an additional property, however this is not
required by this trait: if the CSPRNG’s state is revealed, it should not be
computationally-feasible to reconstruct output prior to this. Some other
generators allow backwards-computation and are considered *reversible*.

Note that this trait is provided for guidance only and cannot guarantee suitability for cryptographic applications. In general it should only be implemented for well-reviewed code implementing well-regarded algorithms.

Note also that use of a `CryptoRng` does not protect against other
weaknesses such as seeding from a weak entropy source or leaking state.

The core of a random number generator.

This trait encapsulates the low-level functionality common to all
generators, and is the “back end”, to be implemented by generators.
End users should normally use the `Rng` trait from the [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand) crate,
which is automatically implemented for every type implementing

`RngCore`.Three different methods for generating random data are provided since the
optimal implementation of each is dependent on the type of generator. There
is no required relationship between the output of each; e.g. many
implementations of [ fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.fill_bytes) consume a whole number of

`u32` or `u64`
values and drop any remaining unused bytes. The same can happen with the
[and](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.next_u32)

`next_u32`[methods, implementations may discard some random bits for efficiency.](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.next_u64)

`next_u64`The [ try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.try_fill_bytes) method is a variant of

[allowing error handling; it is not deemed sufficiently useful to add equivalents for](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.fill_bytes)

`fill_bytes`[or](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.next_u32)

`next_u32`[since the latter methods are almost always used with algorithmic generators (PRNGs), which are normally infallible.](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.next_u64)

`next_u64`Implementers should produce bits uniformly. Pathological RNGs (e.g. always
returning the same value, or never setting certain bits) can break rejection
sampling used by random distributions, and also break other RNGs when
seeding them via [ SeedableRng::from_rng](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html#method.from_rng).

Algorithmic generators implementing [ SeedableRng](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html) should normally have

*portable, reproducible*output, i.e. fix Endianness when converting values to avoid platform differences, and avoid making any changes which affect output (except by communicating that the release has breaking changes).

Typically an RNG will implement only one of the methods available
in this trait directly, then use the helper functions from the
[ impls](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.6.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/impls/index.html) module to implement the other methods.

It is recommended that implementations also implement:

- `Debug`with a custom implementation which- *does not*print any internal state (at least,- `CryptoRng`- `Debug`).
- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`(from Serde), preferably making Serde support optional at the crate level in PRNG libs.
- `Clone`, if possible.
- *never*implement- `Copy`(accidental copies may cause repeated values).
- *do not*implement- `Default`for pseudorandom generators, but instead implement- `SeedableRng`- `Default`.
- `Eq`and- `PartialEq`could be implemented, but are probably not useful.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

A simple example, obviously not generating very *random* output:

```
#![allow(dead_code)]
use rand_core::{RngCore, Error, impls};
struct CountingRng(u64);
impl RngCore for CountingRng {
    fn next_u32(&mut self) -> u32 {
        self.next_u64() as u32
    }
    fn next_u64(&mut self) -> u64 {
        self.0 += 1;
        self.0
    }
    fn fill_bytes(&mut self, dest: &mut [u8]) {
        impls::fill_bytes_via_next(self, dest)
    }
    fn try_fill_bytes(&mut self, dest: &mut [u8]) -> Result<(), Error> {
        Ok(self.fill_bytes(dest))
    }
}
```

`RngCore::try_fill_bytes`This method should guarantee that `dest` is entirely filled
with new data, and may panic if this is impossible
(e.g. reading past the end of a file that is being used as the
source of randomness).

Fill `dest` entirely with random data.

This is the only method which allows an RNG to report errors while
generating random data thus making this the primary method implemented
by external (true) RNGs (e.g. `OsRng`) which can fail. It may be used
directly to generate keys and to seed (infallible) PRNGs.

Other than error handling, this method is identical to [ RngCore::fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.fill_bytes);
thus this may be implemented using

`Ok(self.fill_bytes(dest))` or

}## Expand description

A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.

This trait encapsulates the low-level functionality common to all pseudo-random number generators (PRNGs, or algorithmic generators).

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

Seed type, which is restricted to types mutably-dereferenceable as `u8`
arrays (we recommend `[u8; N]` for some `N`).

It is recommended to seed PRNGs with a seed of at least circa 100 bits,
which means an array of `[u8; 12]` or greater to avoid picking RNGs with
partially overlapping periods.

For cryptographic RNG’s a seed of 256 bits is recommended, `[u8; 32]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-seedablerng-for-rngs-with-large-seeds)Implementing `SeedableRng` for RNGs with large seeds

Note that the required traits `core::default::Default` and
`core::convert::AsMut<u8>` are not implemented for large arrays
`[u8; N]` with `N` > 32. To be able to implement the traits required by
`SeedableRng` for RNGs with such large seeds, the newtype pattern can be
used:

```
use rand_core::SeedableRng;
const N: usize = 64;
pub struct MyRngSeed(pub [u8; N]);
pub struct MyRng(MyRngSeed);
impl Default for MyRngSeed {
    fn default() -> MyRngSeed {
        MyRngSeed([0; N])
    }
}
impl AsMut<[u8]> for MyRngSeed {
    fn as_mut(&mut self) -> &mut [u8] {
        &mut self.0
    }
}
impl SeedableRng for MyRng {
    type Seed = MyRngSeed;
    fn from_seed(seed: MyRngSeed) -> MyRng {
        MyRng(seed)
    }
}
```
## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Create a new PRNG using the given seed.

PRNG implementations are allowed to assume that bits in the seed are
well distributed. That means usually that the number of one and zero
bits are roughly equal, and values like 0, 1 and (size - 1) are unlikely.
Note that many non-cryptographic PRNGs will show poor quality output
if this is not adhered to. If you wish to seed from simple numbers, use
`seed_from_u64` instead.

All PRNG implementations should be reproducible unless otherwise noted:
given a fixed `seed`, the same sequence of output should be produced
on all runs, library versions and architectures (e.g. check endianness).
Any “value-breaking” changes to the generator should require bumping at
least the minor version and documentation of the change.

It is not required that this function yield the same state as a reference implementation of the PRNG given equivalent seed; if necessary another constructor replicating behaviour from a reference implementation can be added.

PRNG implementations should make sure `from_seed` never panics. In the
case that some special values (like an all zero seed) are not viable
seeds it is preferable to map these to alternative constant value(s),
for example `0xBAD5EEDu32` or `0x0DDB1A5E5BAD5EEDu64` (“odd biases? bad
seed”). This is assuming only a small number of values must be rejected.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.6.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/rand_core/lib.rs.html#335)#### fn [seed_from_u64](https://docs.rs#method.seed_from_u64)(state: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.6.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/rand_core/lib.rs.html#335)

#### fn [seed_from_u64](https://docs.rs#method.seed_from_u64)(state: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)) -> Self

Create a new PRNG using a `u64` seed.

This is a convenience-wrapper around `from_seed` to allow construction
of any `SeedableRng` from a simple `u64` value. It is designed such that
low Hamming Weight numbers like 0 and 1 can be used and should still
result in good, independent seeds to the PRNG which is returned.

This **is not suitable for cryptography**, as should be clear given that
the input size is only 64 bits.

Implementations for PRNGs *may* provide their own implementations of
this function, but the default implementation should be good enough for
all purposes. *Changing* the implementation of this function should be
considered a value-breaking change.

Create a new PRNG seeded from another `Rng`.

This may be useful when needing to rapidly seed many PRNGs from a master PRNG, and to allow forking of PRNGs. It may be considered deterministic.

The master PRNG should be at least as high quality as the child PRNGs.
When seeding non-cryptographic child PRNGs, we recommend using a
different algorithm for the master PRNG (ideally a CSPRNG) to avoid
correlations between the child PRNGs. If this is not possible (e.g.
forking using small non-crypto PRNGs) ensure that your PRNG has a good
mixing function on the output or consider use of a hash function with
`from_seed`.

Note that seeding `XorShiftRng` from another `XorShiftRng` provides an
extreme example of what can go wrong: the new PRNG will be a clone
of the parent.

PRNG implementations are allowed to assume that a good RNG is provided
for seeding, and that it is cryptographically secure when appropriate.
As of `rand` 0.7 / `rand_core` 0.5, implementations overriding this
method should ensure the implementation satisfies reproducibility
(in prior versions this was not required).

# subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/subtle/latest/target-redirect/subtle/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#subtle---)subtle

**Pure-Rust traits and utilities for constant-time cryptographic implementations.**

It consists of a `Choice` type, and a collection of traits using `Choice`
instead of `bool` which are intended to execute in constant-time.  The `Choice`
type is a wrapper around a `u8` that holds a `0` or `1`.

`subtle = "2.6"`This crate represents a “best-effort” attempt, since side-channels are ultimately a property of a deployed cryptographic system including the hardware it runs on, not just of software.

The traits are implemented using bitwise operations, and should execute in constant time provided that a) the bitwise operations are constant-time and b) the bitwise operations are not recognized as a conditional assignment and optimized back into a branch.

For a compiler to recognize that bitwise operations represent a conditional
assignment, it needs to know that the value used to generate the bitmasks is
really a boolean `i1` rather than an `i8` byte value. In an attempt to
prevent this refinement, the crate tries to hide the value of a `Choice`’s
inner `u8` by passing it through a volatile read. For more information, see
the *About* section below.

Rust versions from 1.51 or higher have const generics support. You may enable
`const-generics` feautre to have `subtle` traits implemented for arrays `[T; N]`.

Versions prior to `2.2` recommended use of the `nightly` feature to enable an
optimization barrier; this is not required in versions `2.2` and above.

Note: the `subtle` crate contains `debug_assert`s to check invariants during
debug builds. These invariant checks involve secret-dependent branches, and
are not present when compiled in release mode. This crate is intended to be
used in release mode.

[§](https://docs.rs#documentation)Documentation

Documentation is available [here](https://docs.rs/subtle).

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

Rust **1.41** or higher.

Minimum supported Rust version can be changed in the future, but it will be done with a minor version bump.

[§](https://docs.rs#about)About

This library aims to be the Rust equivalent of Go’s `crypto/subtle` module.

Old versions of the optimization barrier in `impl From<u8> for Choice` were
based on Tim Maclean’s [work on  rust-timing-shield](https://www.chosenplaintext.ca/open-source/rust-timing-shield/security),
which attempts to provide a more comprehensive approach for preventing
software side-channels in Rust code.
From version

`2.2`, it was based on Diane Hosfelt and Amber Sprenkels’ work on
“Secret Types in Rust”.`subtle` is authored by isis agora lovecruft and Henry de Valence.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

This code is a low-level library, intended for specific use-cases implementing cryptographic protocols. It represents a best-effort attempt to protect against some software side-channels. Because side-channel resistance is not a property of software alone, but of software together with hardware, any such effort is fundamentally limited.

**USE AT YOUR OWN RISK**

[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! It consists of a `Choice` type, and a collection of traits using `Choice`
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! instead of `bool` which are intended to execute in constant-time.  The `Choice`
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! type is a wrapper around a `u8` that holds a `0` or `1`.
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! ```toml
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! subtle = "2.6"
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! ```
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! This crate represents a “best-effort” attempt, since side-channels
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! are ultimately a property of a deployed cryptographic system
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! including the hardware it runs on, not just of software.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! The traits are implemented using bitwise operations, and should execute in
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! constant time provided that a) the bitwise operations are constant-time and
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! b) the bitwise operations are not recognized as a conditional assignment and
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! optimized back into a branch.
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! For a compiler to recognize that bitwise operations represent a conditional
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! assignment, it needs to know that the value used to generate the bitmasks is
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! really a boolean `i1` rather than an `i8` byte value. In an attempt to
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! prevent this refinement, the crate tries to hide the value of a `Choice`'s
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! inner `u8` by passing it through a volatile read. For more information, see
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! the _About_ section below.
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! Rust versions from 1.51 or higher have const generics support. You may enable
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! `const-generics` feautre to have `subtle` traits implemented for arrays `[T; N]`.
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! Versions prior to `2.2` recommended use of the `nightly` feature to enable an
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! optimization barrier; this is not required in versions `2.2` and above.
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! Note: the `subtle` crate contains `debug_assert`s to check invariants during
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! debug builds. These invariant checks involve secret-dependent branches, and
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! are not present when compiled in release mode. This crate is intended to be
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! used in release mode.
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! ## Documentation
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! Documentation is available [here][docs].
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! ## Minimum Supported Rust Version
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! Rust **1.41** or higher.
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! Minimum supported Rust version can be changed in the future, but it will be done with a minor version bump.
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! ## About
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! This library aims to be the Rust equivalent of Go’s `crypto/subtle` module.
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! Old versions of the optimization barrier in `impl From<u8> for Choice` were
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! based on Tim Maclean's [work on `rust-timing-shield`][rust-timing-shield],
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! which attempts to provide a more comprehensive approach for preventing
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! software side-channels in Rust code.
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! From version `2.2`, it was based on Diane Hosfelt and Amber Sprenkels' work on
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! "Secret Types in Rust".
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! `subtle` is authored by isis agora lovecruft and Henry de Valence.
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! ## Warning
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! This code is a low-level library, intended for specific use-cases implementing
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! cryptographic protocols.  It represents a best-effort attempt to protect
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! against some software side-channels.  Because side-channel resistance is not a
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! property of software alone, but of software together with hardware, any such
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! effort is fundamentally limited.
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! **USE AT YOUR OWN RISK**
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! [docs]: https://docs.rs/subtle
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! [rust-timing-shield]: https://www.chosenplaintext.ca/open-source/rust-timing-shield/security
[90](https://docs.rs#90)

[102](https://docs.rs#102)/// The `Choice` struct represents a choice for use in conditional assignment.
[103](https://docs.rs#103)///
[104](https://docs.rs#104)/// It is a wrapper around a `u8`, which should have the value either `1` (true)
[105](https://docs.rs#105)/// or `0` (false).
[106](https://docs.rs#106)///
[107](https://docs.rs#107)/// The conversion from `u8` to `Choice` passes the value through an optimization
[108](https://docs.rs#108)/// barrier, as a best-effort attempt to prevent the compiler from inferring that
[109](https://docs.rs#109)/// the `Choice` value is a boolean. This strategy is based on Tim Maclean's
[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// [work on `rust-timing-shield`][rust-timing-shield], which attempts to provide
[111](https://docs.rs#111)/// a more comprehensive approach for preventing software side-channels in Rust
[112](https://docs.rs#112)/// code.
[113](https://docs.rs#113)///
[114](https://docs.rs#114)/// The `Choice` struct implements operators for AND, OR, XOR, and NOT, to allow
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// combining `Choice` values. These operations do not short-circuit.
[116](https://docs.rs#116)///
[117](https://docs.rs#117)/// [rust-timing-shield]:
[118](https://docs.rs#118)/// https://www.chosenplaintext.ca/open-source/rust-timing-shield/security
[119](https://docs.rs#119)#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug)]
[120](https://docs.rs#120)pub struct Choice(u8);
[121](https://docs.rs#121)
[122](https://docs.rs#122)impl Choice {
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    /// Unwrap the `Choice` wrapper to reveal the underlying `u8`.
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    ///
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    /// # Note
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    ///
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    /// This function only exists as an **escape hatch** for the rare case
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    /// where it's not possible to use one of the `subtle`-provided
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    /// trait impls.
[130](https://docs.rs#130)    ///
[131](https://docs.rs#131)    /// **To convert a `Choice` to a `bool`, use the `From` implementation instead.**
[132](https://docs.rs#132)    #[inline]
[133](https://docs.rs#133)    pub fn unwrap_u8(&self) -> u8 {
[134](https://docs.rs#134)        self.0
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    }
[136](https://docs.rs#136)}
[137](https://docs.rs#137)
[138](https://docs.rs#138)impl From<Choice> for bool {
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    /// Convert the `Choice` wrapper into a `bool`, depending on whether
[140](https://docs.rs#140)    /// the underlying `u8` was a `0` or a `1`.
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    ///
[142](https://docs.rs#142)    /// # Note
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    ///
[144](https://docs.rs#144)    /// This function exists to avoid having higher-level cryptographic protocol
[145](https://docs.rs#145)    /// implementations duplicating this pattern.
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    ///
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    /// The intended use case for this conversion is at the _end_ of a
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    /// higher-level primitive implementation: for example, in checking a keyed
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    /// MAC, where the verification should happen in constant-time (and thus use
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    /// a `Choice`) but it is safe to return a `bool` at the end of the
[151](https://docs.rs#151)    /// verification.
[152](https://docs.rs#152)    #[inline]
[153](https://docs.rs#153)    fn from(source: Choice) -> bool {
[154](https://docs.rs#154)        debug_assert!((source.0 == 0u8) | (source.0 == 1u8));
[155](https://docs.rs#155)        source.0 != 0
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    }
[157](https://docs.rs#157)}
[158](https://docs.rs#158)
[159](https://docs.rs#159)impl BitAnd for Choice {
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    type Output = Choice;
[161](https://docs.rs#161)    #[inline]
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    fn bitand(self, rhs: Choice) -> Choice {
[163](https://docs.rs#163)        (self.0 & rhs.0).into()
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    }
[165](https://docs.rs#165)}
[166](https://docs.rs#166)
[167](https://docs.rs#167)impl BitAndAssign for Choice {

[169](https://docs.rs#169)    fn bitand_assign(&mut self, rhs: Choice) {
[170](https://docs.rs#170)        *self = *self & rhs;
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    }
[172](https://docs.rs#172)}
[173](https://docs.rs#173)
[174](https://docs.rs#174)impl BitOr for Choice {

[177](https://docs.rs#177)    fn bitor(self, rhs: Choice) -> Choice {
[178](https://docs.rs#178)        (self.0 | rhs.0).into()
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    }
[180](https://docs.rs#180)}

[204](https://docs.rs#204)impl Not for Choice {
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    type Output = Choice;
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    #[inline]
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    fn not(self) -> Choice {
[208](https://docs.rs#208)        (1u8 & (!self.0)).into()
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    }
[210](https://docs.rs#210)}
[211](https://docs.rs#211)
[212](https://docs.rs#212)/// This function is a best-effort attempt to prevent the compiler from knowing
[213](https://docs.rs#213)/// anything about the value of the returned `u8`, other than its type.
[214](https://docs.rs#214)///
[215](https://docs.rs#215)/// Because we want to support stable Rust, we don't have access to inline
[216](https://docs.rs#216)/// assembly or test::black_box, so we use the fact that volatile values will
[217](https://docs.rs#217)/// never be elided to register values.
[218](https://docs.rs#218)///
[219](https://docs.rs#219)/// Note: Rust's notion of "volatile" is subject to change over time. While this
[220](https://docs.rs#220)/// code may break in a non-destructive way in the future, “constant-time” code
[221](https://docs.rs#221)/// is a continually moving target, and this is better than doing nothing.
[222](https://docs.rs#222)#[cfg(not(feature = "core_hint_black_box"))]
[223](https://docs.rs#223)#[inline(never)]
[224](https://docs.rs#224)fn black_box<T: Copy>(input: T) -> T {
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    unsafe {
[226](https://docs.rs#226)        // Optimization barrier
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        //
[228](https://docs.rs#228)        // SAFETY:
[229](https://docs.rs#229)        //   - &input is not NULL because we own input;
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        //   - input is Copy and always live;
[231](https://docs.rs#231)        //   - input is always properly aligned.
[232](https://docs.rs#232)        core::ptr::read_volatile(&input)
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    }
[234](https://docs.rs#234)}
[235](https://docs.rs#235)
[236](https://docs.rs#236)impl From<u8> for Choice {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    #[inline]
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    fn from(input: u8) -> Choice {
[239](https://docs.rs#239)        debug_assert!((input == 0u8) | (input == 1u8));
[240](https://docs.rs#240)
[241](https://docs.rs#241)        // Our goal is to prevent the compiler from inferring that the value held inside the
[242](https://docs.rs#242)        // resulting `Choice` struct is really a `bool` instead of a `u8`.
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        Choice(black_box(input))
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)}
[246](https://docs.rs#246)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)/// An `Eq`-like trait that produces a `Choice` instead of a `bool`.
[248](https://docs.rs#248)///
[249](https://docs.rs#249)/// # Example
[250](https://docs.rs#250)///
[251](https://docs.rs#251)/// ```
[252](https://docs.rs#252)/// use subtle::ConstantTimeEq;
[253](https://docs.rs#253)/// let x: u8 = 5;
[254](https://docs.rs#254)/// let y: u8 = 13;
[255](https://docs.rs#255)///
[256](https://docs.rs#256)/// assert_eq!(x.ct_eq(&y).unwrap_u8(), 0);
[257](https://docs.rs#257)/// assert_eq!(x.ct_eq(&x).unwrap_u8(), 1);
[258](https://docs.rs#258)/// ```
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//
[260](https://docs.rs#260)// #[inline] is specified on these function prototypes to signify that they
[261](https://docs.rs#261)#[allow(unused_attributes)] // should be in the actual implementation
[262](https://docs.rs#262)pub trait ConstantTimeEq {
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    /// Determine if two items are equal.
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    ///
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    /// The `ct_eq` function should execute in constant time.
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    ///
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    /// # Returns
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    ///
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    /// * `Choice(1u8)` if `self == other`;
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    /// * `Choice(0u8)` if `self != other`.
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    #[inline]
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    #[allow(unused_attributes)]
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    fn ct_eq(&self, other: &Self) -> Choice;
[274](https://docs.rs#274)
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    /// Determine if two items are NOT equal.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    ///
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// The `ct_ne` function should execute in constant time.
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    ///
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    /// # Returns
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    ///
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    /// * `Choice(0u8)` if `self == other`;
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    /// * `Choice(1u8)` if `self != other`.
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    #[inline]
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    fn ct_ne(&self, other: &Self) -> Choice {
[285](https://docs.rs#285)        !self.ct_eq(other)
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    }
[287](https://docs.rs#287)}
[288](https://docs.rs#288)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)impl<T: ConstantTimeEq> ConstantTimeEq for [T] {
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    /// Check whether two slices of `ConstantTimeEq` types are equal.
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    ///
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    /// # Note
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    ///
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    /// This function short-circuits if the lengths of the input slices
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    /// are different.  Otherwise, it should execute in time independent
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    /// of the slice contents.
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    ///
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    /// Since arrays coerce to slices, this function works with fixed-size arrays:
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    ///
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    /// ```
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    /// # use subtle::ConstantTimeEq;
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    /// #
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    /// let a: [u8; 8] = [0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7];
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    /// let b: [u8; 8] = [0,1,2,3,0,1,2,3];
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    ///
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    /// let a_eq_a = a.ct_eq(&a);
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    /// let a_eq_b = a.ct_eq(&b);
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    ///
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    /// assert_eq!(a_eq_a.unwrap_u8(), 1);
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    /// assert_eq!(a_eq_b.unwrap_u8(), 0);
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    /// ```
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    #[inline]
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    fn ct_eq(&self, _rhs: &[T]) -> Choice {
[314](https://docs.rs#314)        let len = self.len();
[315](https://docs.rs#315)
[316](https://docs.rs#316)        // Short-circuit on the *lengths* of the slices, not their
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        // contents.
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        if len != _rhs.len() {
[319](https://docs.rs#319)            return Choice::from(0);
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        }
[321](https://docs.rs#321)
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        // This loop shouldn't be shortcircuitable, since the compiler
[323](https://docs.rs#323)        // shouldn't be able to reason about the value of the `u8`
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        // unwrapped from the `ct_eq` result.
[325](https://docs.rs#325)        let mut x = 1u8;
[326](https://docs.rs#326)        for (ai, bi) in self.iter().zip(_rhs.iter()) {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)            x &= ai.ct_eq(bi).unwrap_u8();
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        }
[329](https://docs.rs#329)
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        x.into()
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    }
[332](https://docs.rs#332)}
[333](https://docs.rs#333)
[334](https://docs.rs#334)impl ConstantTimeEq for Choice {
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    #[inline]
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    fn ct_eq(&self, rhs: &Choice) -> Choice {
[337](https://docs.rs#337)        !(*self ^ *rhs)
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    }
[339](https://docs.rs#339)}
[340](https://docs.rs#340)
[341](https://docs.rs#341)/// Given the bit-width `$bit_width` and the corresponding primitive
[342](https://docs.rs#342)/// unsigned and signed types `$t_u` and `$t_i` respectively, generate
[343](https://docs.rs#343)/// an `ConstantTimeEq` implementation.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)macro_rules! generate_integer_equal {
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    ($t_u:ty, $t_i:ty, $bit_width:expr) => {
[346](https://docs.rs#346)        impl ConstantTimeEq for $t_u {
[347](https://docs.rs#347)            #[inline]
[348](https://docs.rs#348)            fn ct_eq(&self, other: &$t_u) -> Choice {
[349](https://docs.rs#349)                // x == 0 if and only if self == other
[350](https://docs.rs#350)                let x: $t_u = self ^ other;
[351](https://docs.rs#351)
[352](https://docs.rs#352)                // If x == 0, then x and -x are both equal to zero;
[353](https://docs.rs#353)                // otherwise, one or both will have its high bit set.
[354](https://docs.rs#354)                let y: $t_u = (x | x.wrapping_neg()) >> ($bit_width - 1);
[355](https://docs.rs#355)
[356](https://docs.rs#356)                // Result is the opposite of the high bit (now shifted to low).
[357](https://docs.rs#357)                ((y ^ (1 as $t_u)) as u8).into()
[358](https://docs.rs#358)            }
[359](https://docs.rs#359)        }
[360](https://docs.rs#360)        impl ConstantTimeEq for $t_i {
[361](https://docs.rs#361)            #[inline]
[362](https://docs.rs#362)            fn ct_eq(&self, other: &$t_i) -> Choice {
[363](https://docs.rs#363)                // Bitcast to unsigned and call that implementation.
[364](https://docs.rs#364)                (*self as $t_u).ct_eq(&(*other as $t_u))
[365](https://docs.rs#365)            }
[366](https://docs.rs#366)        }
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    };
[368](https://docs.rs#368)}
[369](https://docs.rs#369)
[370](https://docs.rs#370)generate_integer_equal!(u8, i8, 8);
[371](https://docs.rs#371)generate_integer_equal!(u16, i16, 16);
[372](https://docs.rs#372)generate_integer_equal!(u32, i32, 32);
[373](https://docs.rs#373)generate_integer_equal!(u64, i64, 64);
[374](https://docs.rs#374)#[cfg(feature = "i128")]
[375](https://docs.rs#375)generate_integer_equal!(u128, i128, 128);
[376](https://docs.rs#376)generate_integer_equal!(usize, isize, ::core::mem::size_of::<usize>() * 8);

[378](https://docs.rs#378)/// `Ordering` is `#[repr(i8)]` making it possible to leverage `i8::ct_eq`.
[379](https://docs.rs#379)impl ConstantTimeEq for cmp::Ordering {
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    #[inline]
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    fn ct_eq(&self, other: &Self) -> Choice {
[382](https://docs.rs#382)        (*self as i8).ct_eq(&(*other as i8))
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    }
[384](https://docs.rs#384)}
[385](https://docs.rs#385)
[386](https://docs.rs#386)/// A type which can be conditionally selected in constant time.
[387](https://docs.rs#387)///
[388](https://docs.rs#388)/// This trait also provides generic implementations of conditional
[389](https://docs.rs#389)/// assignment and conditional swaps.
[390](https://docs.rs#390)//
[391](https://docs.rs#391)// #[inline] is specified on these function prototypes to signify that they
[392](https://docs.rs#392)#[allow(unused_attributes)] // should be in the actual implementation
[393](https://docs.rs#393)pub trait ConditionallySelectable: Copy {
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    /// Select `a` or `b` according to `choice`.
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    ///
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    /// # Returns
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    ///
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    /// * `a` if `choice == Choice(0)`;
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    /// * `b` if `choice == Choice(1)`.
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    ///
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    /// This function should execute in constant time.
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    ///
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    /// # Example
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    ///
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    /// ```
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    /// use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    /// #
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    /// # fn main() {
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    /// let x: u8 = 13;
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// let y: u8 = 42;
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    ///
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    /// let z = u8::conditional_select(&x, &y, 0.into());
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    /// assert_eq!(z, x);
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    /// let z = u8::conditional_select(&x, &y, 1.into());
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    /// assert_eq!(z, y);
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    /// # }
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    /// ```
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    #[inline]
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    #[allow(unused_attributes)]
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    fn conditional_select(a: &Self, b: &Self, choice: Choice) -> Self;
[421](https://docs.rs#421)
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    /// Conditionally assign `other` to `self`, according to `choice`.
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    ///
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    /// This function should execute in constant time.
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    ///
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    /// # Example
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    ///
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// ```
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    /// use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    /// #
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    /// # fn main() {
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    /// let mut x: u8 = 13;
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    /// let mut y: u8 = 42;
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    ///
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    /// x.conditional_assign(&y, 0.into());
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    /// assert_eq!(x, 13);
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    /// x.conditional_assign(&y, 1.into());
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// assert_eq!(x, 42);
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    /// # }
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    /// ```
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    #[inline]
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    fn conditional_assign(&mut self, other: &Self, choice: Choice) {
[443](https://docs.rs#443)        *self = Self::conditional_select(self, other, choice);
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    }
[445](https://docs.rs#445)
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    /// Conditionally swap `self` and `other` if `choice == 1`; otherwise,
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    /// reassign both unto themselves.
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    ///
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    /// This function should execute in constant time.
[450](https://docs.rs#450)    ///
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    /// # Example
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    ///
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    /// ```
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    /// use subtle::ConditionallySelectable;
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    /// #
[456](https://docs.rs#456)    /// # fn main() {
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    /// let mut x: u8 = 13;
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    /// let mut y: u8 = 42;
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    ///
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    /// u8::conditional_swap(&mut x, &mut y, 0.into());
[461](https://docs.rs#461)    /// assert_eq!(x, 13);
[462](https://docs.rs#462)    /// assert_eq!(y, 42);
[463](https://docs.rs#463)    /// u8::conditional_swap(&mut x, &mut y, 1.into());
[464](https://docs.rs#464)    /// assert_eq!(x, 42);
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    /// assert_eq!(y, 13);
[466](https://docs.rs#466)    /// # }
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    /// ```
[468](https://docs.rs#468)    #[inline]
[469](https://docs.rs#469)    fn conditional_swap(a: &mut Self, b: &mut Self, choice: Choice) {
[470](https://docs.rs#470)        let t: Self = *a;
[471](https://docs.rs#471)        a.conditional_assign(&b, choice);
[472](https://docs.rs#472)        b.conditional_assign(&t, choice);
[473](https://docs.rs#473)    }
[474](https://docs.rs#474)}

[509](https://docs.rs#509)macro_rules! generate_integer_conditional_select {
[510](https://docs.rs#510)    ($($t:tt)*) => ($(
[511](https://docs.rs#511)        impl ConditionallySelectable for $t {
[512](https://docs.rs#512)            #[inline]
[513](https://docs.rs#513)            fn conditional_select(a: &Self, b: &Self, choice: Choice) -> Self {
[514](https://docs.rs#514)                // if choice = 0, mask = (-0) = 0000...0000
[515](https://docs.rs#515)                // if choice = 1, mask = (-1) = 1111...1111
[516](https://docs.rs#516)                let mask = -(choice.unwrap_u8() as to_signed_int!($t)) as $t;
[517](https://docs.rs#517)                a ^ (mask & (a ^ b))
[518](https://docs.rs#518)            }
[519](https://docs.rs#519)
[520](https://docs.rs#520)            #[inline]
[521](https://docs.rs#521)            fn conditional_assign(&mut self, other: &Self, choice: Choice) {
[522](https://docs.rs#522)                // if choice = 0, mask = (-0) = 0000...0000
[523](https://docs.rs#523)                // if choice = 1, mask = (-1) = 1111...1111
[524](https://docs.rs#524)                let mask = -(choice.unwrap_u8() as to_signed_int!($t)) as $t;
[525](https://docs.rs#525)                *self ^= mask & (*self ^ *other);
[526](https://docs.rs#526)            }
[527](https://docs.rs#527)
[528](https://docs.rs#528)            #[inline]
[529](https://docs.rs#529)            fn conditional_swap(a: &mut Self, b: &mut Self, choice: Choice) {
[530](https://docs.rs#530)                // if choice = 0, mask = (-0) = 0000...0000
[531](https://docs.rs#531)                // if choice = 1, mask = (-1) = 1111...1111
[532](https://docs.rs#532)                let mask = -(choice.unwrap_u8() as to_signed_int!($t)) as $t;
[533](https://docs.rs#533)                let t = mask & (*a ^ *b);
[534](https://docs.rs#534)                *a ^= t;
[535](https://docs.rs#535)                *b ^= t;
[536](https://docs.rs#536)            }
[537](https://docs.rs#537)         }
[538](https://docs.rs#538)    )*)
[539](https://docs.rs#539)}

[548](https://docs.rs#548)/// `Ordering` is `#[repr(i8)]` where:
[549](https://docs.rs#549)///
[550](https://docs.rs#550)/// - `Less` => -1
[551](https://docs.rs#551)/// - `Equal` => 0
[552](https://docs.rs#552)/// - `Greater` => 1
[553](https://docs.rs#553)///
[554](https://docs.rs#554)/// Given this, it's possible to operate on orderings as if they're integers,
[555](https://docs.rs#555)/// which allows leveraging conditional masking for predication.
[556](https://docs.rs#556)impl ConditionallySelectable for cmp::Ordering {
[557](https://docs.rs#557)    fn conditional_select(a: &Self, b: &Self, choice: Choice) -> Self {
[558](https://docs.rs#558)        let a = *a as i8;
[559](https://docs.rs#559)        let b = *b as i8;
[560](https://docs.rs#560)        let ret = i8::conditional_select(&a, &b, choice);
[561](https://docs.rs#561)
[562](https://docs.rs#562)        // SAFETY: `Ordering` is `#[repr(i8)]` and `ret` has been assigned to
[563](https://docs.rs#563)        // a value which was originally a valid `Ordering` then cast to `i8`
[564](https://docs.rs#564)        unsafe { *((&ret as *const _) as *const cmp::Ordering) }
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    }
[566](https://docs.rs#566)}

[568](https://docs.rs#568)impl ConditionallySelectable for Choice {

[571](https://docs.rs#571)        Choice(u8::conditional_select(&a.0, &b.0, choice))
[572](https://docs.rs#572)    }

[594](https://docs.rs#594)/// A type which can be conditionally negated in constant time.

[596](https://docs.rs#596)/// # Note
[597](https://docs.rs#597)///
[598](https://docs.rs#598)/// A generic implementation of `ConditionallyNegatable` is provided
[599](https://docs.rs#599)/// for types `T` which are `ConditionallySelectable` and have `Neg`

[601](https://docs.rs#601)//
[602](https://docs.rs#602)// #[inline] is specified on these function prototypes to signify that they

[604](https://docs.rs#604)pub trait ConditionallyNegatable {
[605](https://docs.rs#605)    /// Negate `self` if `choice == Choice(1)`; otherwise, leave it
[606](https://docs.rs#606)    /// unchanged.
[607](https://docs.rs#607)    ///
[608](https://docs.rs#608)    /// This function should execute in constant time.
[609](https://docs.rs#609)    #[inline]
[610](https://docs.rs#610)    #[allow(unused_attributes)]
[611](https://docs.rs#611)    fn conditional_negate(&mut self, choice: Choice);
[612](https://docs.rs#612)}

[614](https://docs.rs#614)impl<T> ConditionallyNegatable for T
[615](https://docs.rs#615)where
[616](https://docs.rs#616)    T: ConditionallySelectable,
[617](https://docs.rs#617)    for<'a> &'a T: Neg<Output = T>,
[618](https://docs.rs#618){
[619](https://docs.rs#619)    #[inline]
[620](https://docs.rs#620)    fn conditional_negate(&mut self, choice: Choice) {
[621](https://docs.rs#621)        // Need to cast to eliminate mutability
[622](https://docs.rs#622)        let self_neg: T = -(self as &T);
